excerpt: Contribute to crocone/flying-test development by creating an account on GitHub.
content_html:
Flight test stand — stages 1–6

Live demo: https://crocone.github.io/flying-test/ — the whole stand runs in your browser. Building a vehicle from a description or an image needs your own server and AI key (npm run api), so it is switched off in the demo; pick one of the examples.

The check scripts (npm run check, npm run physics) print outcomes in Russian: ПРОЙДЕН = PASS, РАСХОЖДЕНИЕ = DIVERGENCE (a known, explained mismatch with measurements), ПРОВАЛ = FAIL, СПРАВОЧНО = INFO. The stand UI has a Russian/English switch.

R22 in free flight and its stress tests to FAR 27 (2026-11-24)

VALIDATE_ONLY=helistress npm run physics -- --validate   # the helicopter series vs. the R22 POH and Robinson safety notices (~10 min)
VALIDATE_ONLY=heli,r22 npm run physics -- --validate     # earlier R22 checks, re-run after the rotor changes
npm run check   # everything together (both stress sections included): 505 checks — 389 pass, 115 "DIVERGENCE", 1 failure: three new R22 names had no English translation — fixed after the run and checked separately

Free flight

Until now the helicopter was only ever tested with its body held (hover — vertical only, forward flight — in a "tunnel"). For the stress tests it now flies freely in all six degrees of freedom:

  • Tail rotor as a force (Sim.tailRotorFree, tailRotor.at, tailRotor.channel). The pedals set the tail-rotor blade pitch; thrust comes from BEMT with the flow through the disc (sideslip and yaw rate change it — this is what gives the tail rotor its weathercock effect), and it acts on the boom. Its power is taken from the main rotor shaft, as before. Programmes with the body held keep the old model (thrust = rotor torque / arm).
  • Body rates in the flapping equation. The inertial moment about each hinge is now summed over the blade elements, the same way the loads are: Iβ·β̈ = M + M_g − Σ m·(d × (ω̇ × d + ω × (ω × d)))·ê, with ω the hub's rotation together with the body. When the fuselage pitches, the disc lags behind the shaft and damps it (checked: at q = 0.2 rad/s the disc tilts 0.38° forward relative to the shaft; theory a₁ = −16q/(γΩ) gives about 0.7° for an estimated Lock number of 4.5). Gravity in the flapping equation is now g − a_hub: in a pull-up the blades cone up.
  • No false gyroscope. The blades are rigid Rapier bodies with the flapping laid over them, so when the fuselage turned, Rapier turned the whole spinning rotor with it and sent its gyroscopic moment into the fuselage through the joint — hundreds of N·m per 0.1 rad/s, a false pitch-roll coupling that made free hover diverge. A real hinge cannot transmit it; that moment is now applied to the blade body itself.
  • R22 geometry from the maintenance manual drawing (ch. 16, fig. 16-2, scaled by the 259 in dimension): horizontal stabiliser 34 in span, about 8 in chord, 148 in behind the mast, set 2.8–3.3° nose down; upper and lower fins about 18 and 17 in tall; tail rotor 174 in behind the mast (POH: 172), 73 in above ground.
  • The centre of gravity was 5.4 in behind the mast — outside the R22 envelope (POH fig. on p. 2-5: about 95–102 in, mast at station 100). With the body held it did not matter; in free flight it was a 1000 N·m nose-up moment. The cabin mass is now 0.215 m forward, putting the CG at station 98 (an estimate inside the envelope).
  • The engine as a torque with a power limit. In free flight the mast joint has no Rapier motor (Rapier's velocity motor holds rpm with any torque — the first free runs flew on up to 250 kW with a 97.7 kW engine). A governor holds 104 % rpm with torque up to available power / Ω (minus transmission losses); the tail rotor is driven from the same shaft. When the demand is higher, the rotor rpm droops; in a pull-up it rises above 104 % — the engine cannot brake it.
  • A pilot autopilot (src/core/helipilot.ts): collective holds vertical speed, cyclic holds attitude with rate damping, attitude is set by speed and drift, pedals hold heading or zero sideslip.

Free flight against the held "tunnel" trim (which matched Robinson's power data earlier): 60 kt — 42–46 kW vs. 44.8, collective 11.3–11.6° vs. 11.45°; 90 kt — about 77 kW vs. 73.6, collective 12.9–13.9° vs. 13.3°.

The series

The helicopter takes off, hovers, accelerates, and is moved to 600 m. Criteria where the rules or the POH give one; the rest are measurements. Blade strength in forward flight stays for reference only (see "R22 in forward flight": equivalent spar, hub suspension not published — the root margin is below 1 already in level flight at 90 kt), so blades do not break in this programme and the verdict is not based on it.

Test (rule) What is done R22, model
Hover out of ground effect 600 m, 1370 lb ✅ 72.4 kW of 97.7; 43 % pedal travel left
Cyclic pull-up at 0.6 / 0.9 VNE (§27.337) aft cyclic to +3.5 g, collective fixed 2.2 / 3.2 g — the rotor stalls first (the R22 design limit is not published); rpm rises to 104 %
Low-G pushover (prohibited on the R22) forward cyclic to 0.2 g, lateral cyclic and pedals fixed rolls right at 22 °/s — as the POH and SN-11 warn
30 ft/s vertical gust (§27.341) hover / 0.6 VNE / VNE, controls fixed through the gust 1.29 / 1.74 / 1.91 g
Full pedal in 0.2 s (§27.351) hover / 0.6 VNE 166 °/s; 81° sideslip at 61 kt (the rule allows up to 90°)
Engine failure at 0.9 VNE (§27.143(e)) controls fixed 1 s, then autorotation at 65 kt ✅ 83 % rpm after 1 s, steady 96–104 % (POH: 90–110 %); 1340 ft/min (SN-38: usually below 1500)
1.1 VNE (§27.175, AC 27-1) 112 kt ✅ 40 % forward cyclic left; not enough power for level flight — flown at −4 m/s at full power, rpm 100 %, 7.5 % of blade sections stalled, advancing tip M 0.78. Held level instead, the collective "eats" the rpm (down to 91 %, below the 97 % low-rpm horn) and retreating-blade stall grows to a third of the disc

Limitations

  • The engine failure is the last test: the programme ends in autorotation.
  • No vortex ring and no ground contact on the skids, so the vortex ring and dynamic rollover tests are not in the series.
  • The governor is ideal (no lag, no throttle correlator); the engine power does not depend on rpm. A low-rpm test (raising the collective with the throttle fixed) is not in the series.
  • The flapping hinges are at the hub centre. The real R22 has a teetering hinge plus coning hinges slightly off the axis (offset not published). With the hinge at the centre, the blade root 0.45 m out carries the hinge shear × 0.45 m in bending — the hover blade margin is now 3.3 (it was 6.4 with the old flapping equation, which passed a moment "through" the hinge).
  • The R22 load factor limit, transient rpm minimum and teeter stop angle are not published — reported as measured, without a pass/fail.
  • The main-rotor wake on the stabiliser and fins is not modelled.
  • Validation: 5 checks against what a certified R22 does (hover OGE at max weight, autorotation rpm and sink rate, right roll in low G, forward cyclic left at 1.1 VNE) — all pass.

Stress tests to FAR 23 — and what they exposed in the physics (2026-11-24)

VALIDATE_ONLY=stress npm run physics -- --validate          # the stress programme on the Cessna 172S vs. POH and the rules (~7 min)
VALIDATE_ONLY=sixdof,cessna npm run physics -- --validate   # roll on full aileron, POH tables — re-checked after the aerodynamics changes
npm run check   # see the R22 section above for the latest full run (505 checks); the run before the helicopter work: 500 checks — 384 pass, 115 "DIVERGENCE", 1 failure ("influence calculation within 60 s": 64.5 s with the CPU busy, 37.8 s alone)

The programme

New programme "Stress tests (FAR 23)" for fixed-wing aircraft (stress in src/core/programs.ts). Sources for the list and the criteria are in data/stress-tests.md. The aircraft takes off, then flies a series of certification manoeuvres at 1500 m. Each manoeuvre has a target from the rules, a measurement and a pass/fail. The strength criterion everywhere is a safety margin of at least 1.5 at the limit load (§23.303, §23.305). In the browser, setup and recovery between manoeuvres are fast-forwarded; take-off and the manoeuvres themselves play in real time.

Test (rule) What is done Cessna 172S, model
+3.8 g at VA (§23.333, §23.337) entry at 1.05·VA = 108 kt, pull to the limit, 1 s 3.55 g at 107 kt — the wing stalls first (that is what VA means); margin 1.92
+3.8 g at VC = 33·√(W/S) = 127 kt pull, 1 s 3.79 g, margin 1.84
−1.52 g at VC (§23.337(b)) push, 1 s −1.67 g (the autopilot overshoots by 10 %), margin 3.93
±50 ft/s gusts at VC (§23.333(c), §23.341) 1 − cos gust over 25 chords, frozen in the air; elevator fixed 3.82 / −1.90 g; the rule's formula gives 3.83 / −1.83; margin 1.80. With a gust applied to the whole aircraft at once it was 3.34 / −1.25
Checked pitch manoeuvre at VA (§23.423) full aft stick to the limit, then forward 3.31 / −0.63 g, margin 2.09
Rolling pull-out (§23.349, §23.455) from a 60° turn at 2/3 of the limit g, full aileron to roll out 82 °/s, margin 2.78
Full rudder at VA (§23.351) step to the peak sideslip, then neutral 13.2°, margin 6.85
Dive to VD = 1.4·VC = 178 kt (§23.251, §23.33) full throttle, rpm held at the red line; 1 s at VD; pull-out 175 kt; windmilling 2940 rpm with the throttle closed (110 % = 2970 allowed); flutter far away
Wings-level stall (§23.201) 1 kt/s, power off, controls fixed for 1 s at the break 52 kt (POH: 53 KCAS); bank 5°; 55 m lost (POH: up to 230 ft = 70 m)
Turning stall, 30° (§23.203) 1 kt/s 54.5 kt (POH: 57 KCAS); bank −24…+36° (allowed 60/30)
Accelerated turning stall (§23.203) 4 kt/s with rising g 62.5 kt; bank −24…+43°
One-turn spin (§23.221) full aft stick and rudder at the break not reproduced: the model settles into a spiral (see limitations)

What the tests found in the physics

The first runs gave margins that jumped by ±30 % from one sample to the next and a roll rate twice the real one. The cause was in the physics, not in the tests:

  1. Wing bending had no air damping in free flight. The aerodynamic damping of the first bending mode was computed from the wind-tunnel flow, which is zero when the aircraft flies freely. So the wing rang at 3 % damping after every control input. Now damping follows the current airspeed: about 10–15 % for the Cessna wing in flight (sim.ts, elasticInfo and the load step).
  2. In-plane wing bending went through the narrow spar only. When the wing has a torsion box, in-plane bending is now carried by the whole box: spar, upper and lower skins, rear web (section.ts). Stiffness is 17× higher, the spurious 4 Hz in-plane ringing is gone, and the margin in the checked manoeuvre went from 1.41 to over 1.9.
  3. One uniform induced angle per wing half → a lifting line. Each strip of the main wings is now a horseshoe vortex. Induced angles come from Biot–Savart over all strips of both halves, solved each step by a Newton step (plain iteration diverges on the saw-tooth mode). Before, lift did not fall off at the tip and antisymmetric loading (ailerons, roll rate) was barely damped by downwash. Flapping wings keep the previous model: their wake is unsteady, and a quasi-steady lifting line made the Snowbird check worse (thrust margin 0.54 → 0.40 against a measured 0.92). The "straight wing in a tunnel" check used a single half-wing and the full-wing formula: the old model silently assumed the missing half. It is now a full rectangular wing of aspect ratio 10, compared with an independent method — Glauert's Fourier-series solution of the lifting line: lift +2.2 %, induced drag within 0.4 %.
  4. Control surfaces followed thin-airfoil theory at any deflection. With control.chordFrac (c_f/c) set, two DATCOM corrections are added (sec. 6.1.1.1, digitised in Roskam Part VI): the viscous one (a real surface is weaker than theory) and the nonlinear K'(δ) for large deflections. The method reproduces NACA TR 661 (23012, 0.2c flap) to ±0.03 in Δc_l up to 20°. Set for the Cessna aileron, elevator and rudder.
  5. The gust hit the whole aircraft at once. It was a uniform vertical wind, so the tail felt it together with the wing. Now a gust is frozen in the air (sim.gustAt): the aircraft flies through it, and every strip of the wing and the tail sees it at its own position — the tail l_t/V later. That is how the rules' gust alleviation factor is derived.
  6. Crew vibration in the stress programme. The vibration measure (ISO 2631, RMS over 2 s) is meant for sustained shaking; gusts and abrupt controls are one-off jolts, already assessed by the g-load by axis and the Brinkley impact model. In this programme vibration is measured only in steady flight between manoeuvres (a note in the report says so). The recovery after each manoeuvre now starts with a smooth 1.5 s unload — the autopilot used to push from 3.7 g to 0.2 g in about a second.
Quantity Before After Reference
Aileron power C_lδa, 1/rad 0.48 0.30 JSBSim 0.23, UIUC 0.18 (calculations)
Roll damping C_lp −0.62 −0.48 JSBSim −0.47
pb/2V on full aileron, 104 kt 0.24 0.18 Cessna 177B in flight 0.09 (NASA CR-2337) — divergence
Cruise power vs. POH table, mean −6.6 % −2.8 % POH fig. 5-8
Rate of climb, 0 / 8000 ft +15 / +16 % +10 / +5 % POH fig. 5-7
Stall, flaps up −0.4 % +0.4 % POH 53 KCAS
POH section of the checks (24) 16 pass, 8 divergences 14 pass, 10 divergences climb at 8000 ft now passes; top speed at 8000 ft (−4.3 %, limited by the 2700 rpm of the "light" propeller) and three cruise rpm rows went just over tolerance

Why it diverges

  • Roll rate: still twice the Cessna 177B in flight. That is a different aircraft (cantilever wing, its own ailerons). In the test the pedals were held, so adverse yaw built 8–11° of sideslip, which slows the roll through dihedral effect. The model has no aileron hinge gaps and almost no adverse yaw. The calculated C172 models give 0.12–0.15.
  • Propeller rpm in cruise is 2–4 % high (the known "light propeller", see the propeller section). With the lower drag of the lifting line it shows up in more rows: 3 of the cruise rpm checks went just over their 2 % tolerance.
  • The 30° turning stall is 4.4 % below the POH: the programme detects the stall by the share of stalled strips (30 %), the certification test by the nose drop or the stick reaching its stop.

Limitations

  • The spin is not reproduced. With full aft stick and rudder the model sits at α ≈ 14° in a spiral. Autorotation needs rotary-balance data for the wing beyond the stall, which strip theory does not have. The step is reported as "not tested".
  • Strength margins belong to the equivalent cantilever spar (its wall is an estimate; the strut is not in the strength calculation). They are not a check of the real airframe.
  • The autopilot is a test pilot with limits: at VA the wing stalls at 3.55 g before reaching 3.8 g, and −1.52 g overshoots to −1.67 g. Both are shown as measured.
  • The helicopter series is described in the next section up (R22 in free flight).

Human: power vs. duration, g-loads by axis and time (2026-11-23)

VALIDATE_ONLY=human npm run physics -- --validate   # checks for this section (seconds)
npm run check   # everything together: 493 checks — 382 pass, 111 "DIVERGENCE", no failures

The full run had one failure: a verdict text contained a number that was not in the telemetry. It was fixed after the run and checked separately. The new crew model did not change the verdicts of earlier tests.

What was added to the core

  • Human as an engine (powerplant.engine: { type: 'human', level: 'healthy' | 'champion', durationS }).
    • Available power is what a person can sustain for a given time. Source: NASA SP-3006 (1973) curves, fig. 18-15: healthy men and champions.
    • Endurance in the report comes from the inverse curve: how long the person can last at the required power.
  • Crew g-loads by body axis and duration (src/core/crew.ts, CrewLoad). Previously there was a g-load module checked against a single threshold; now:
    • Sustained. Averages along ±Gx, Gy, ±Gz over windows from 1 to 1200 s are compared against two curves:
      • the NASA-STD-3001 limit (rev. C, 2022) for a healthy crew — "severe";
      • average tolerance of healthy people (Chambers 1963, via SP-3006) — "dangerous".
    • Loss of consciousness (G-LOC). +Gz averaged over 5 s from 5.4 g (Cochran 1954, unprotected) — "no one left to fly the aircraft".
    • Impact. Brinkley model: spinal response along three axes, coefficients from NASA/TM-2013-217380. The combined axis index β is compared with NASA limits for low (< 0.5 %) and moderate (0.5–5 %) injury risk.
    • The old "sustained / peak g-load" values remain in the telemetry for comparison. The crew verdict names whatever exceeded its limit: axis, window, limit, impact, vibration.

What the checks showed

Check Result
Healthy human power (SP-3006) vs. Whitt & Wilson 1982, 5 points pass, 0–4 %
Champion power vs. professional cyclists (Pinot & Grappe 2014, Valenzuela 2022, Gallo 2022, Wilkie 1960), 14 points 10 pass; 4 divergences at efforts of 30 s – 5 min: modern racers are 11–18 % higher
Daedalus: 3.1 W/kg for 6 hours info: extending the curve gives 227 W (beyond the data)
+Gz tolerance vs. test pilots (Chambers & Hitchcock 1963): 9 g — 8 s, 8 g — 29 s, 6 g — 157 s 2 pass (3 and 2 %), 1 divergence +16 % at 8 s
Brinkley model vs. rocket sled tests (Stapp; SP-3006), 7 tests all tests with injury are above the low-risk limit: pass

Info. The Brinkley model also places impacts survived without harm in the moderate-risk band: −Gx 45 g for 0.09 s and +Gx 30 g for 0.11 s. NASA limits are for design, with margin. The pulse shapes in the tests were not recorded: a trapezoid is assumed.

Loss of consciousness across different centrifuges: Cochran 5.4 ± 0.9 g, Zarriello 5.3 ± 0.8, Kasture 4.89 ± 0.67, Chiang 5.1 ± 0.9. The others use different endpoints: loss of peripheral or central vision, which comes earlier.

Limitations

  • Human power does not depend on altitude. Above 1500 m aerobic power drops; in the model it does not. Body mass is not given in the SP-3006 curves: power is absolute, in watts.
  • The NASA limit assumes a restraint harness and an anti-g suit. Chambers tolerance is voluntary, for healthy subjects. There is no tolerance curve for Gy; the NASA emergency limit is used instead.
  • Consciousness under negative g (−Gz) is not assessed separately — only via the curves.
  • The occupant sits facing forward; body axes coincide with the airframe axes.

Structure: wing flutter and divergence, laminated composites (2026-11-23)

VALIDATE_ONLY=structure npm run physics -- --validate   # checks for this section (seconds)
npm run check   # everything together: 470 checks — 364 pass, 106 "DIVERGENCE" (full run 2026-11-23 — 469 checks; the strut-braced Cessna flutter check was added after it and passed separately; the "influence calculation within 60 s" check did not fit in that run — 130 s with the CPU busy with other programs)

What was added to the core

  • Wing flutter and divergence (src/core/aeroelastic.ts).

    • A beam with an elastic axis; mode shapes by the finite element method (bending — Euler–Bernoulli beam, torsion — a rod, coupling — via the offset of the center of mass); the four lowest are used.
    • Supports: the root is clamped or hinged; the strut (structure.strut) is a vertical support at its attachment point on the chord: it couples deflection with twist.
    • Theodorsen unsteady aerodynamics, strip by strip.
    • Solved by the p-k method: at each speed the roots of the characteristic polynomial are found. Flutter is the speed where an oscillation stops decaying. Divergence is where torsion loses static stability.

  • Flutter in the stand (Sim.flutterInfo). Computed for a stationary wing with a specified torsion box structure.torsionBox — the skin between the spars that carries torsion. From the part's structure the following are taken:

    • EI — of the spar;
    • GJ — of the torsion box, by the Bredt formula;
    • elastic axis — the middle of the torsion box;
    • mass distribution — the spar at sparAt, the skin along the chord.

    Without a torsion box the torsional stiffness is unknown, and flutter is not checked.

  • Cessna 172S: torsion box and strut are estimates (assumptions "Wing torsion box skin" and "Strut attachment"). There is no data: the Cessna structural repair manual (SESR04) gives only materials; there are no wing stiffnesses or frequency measurements. Spars at 20 and 65 % chord, skin 0.020 in, strut to the front spar at 2.6 m from the centerline, root hinged. Result: no wing flutter up to 270 m/s, divergence from 690 m/s for any combination of estimates (skin 0.016–0.025 in, spars ±5 % chord, strut ±0.3 m). This is a plausibility check: the aircraft is certified, and the regulations require freedom from flutter up to 1.2·V_D ≈ 112 m/s. Without the strut the same cantilever diverges at 192 m/s, and the first frequency drops from 12.8 to 6.5 Hz. Aileron flutter (on the real aircraft they are mass-balanced) is not computed.

  • Flutter in the verdict. If the test speed reached the flutter or divergence speed — "Breaks up". If the margin is below 20 %, a warning (CS-23.629 requires 1.2 times the design dive speed). The report has a line "Wing flutter and divergence".

  • Laminated composite (src/core/laminate.ts, structure.layup: fractions of 0°, ±45°, 90° plies).

    • Stiffness — by classical laminate theory.
    • Strength — by maximum strain in ply axes, with cracked plies switched off: fibers break — the laminate has failed; the matrix cracks — the ply loses transverse stiffness and the load is redistributed.
    • Without a layup, the composite is unidirectional along the span, as before.
    • Materials now have Yt and Yc — ply strength transverse to the fibers.

What the checks showed

Check Model Measured Result
Goland wing (computational benchmark) 137.0 m/s, 68 rad/s 137 m/s, ≈70 rad/s pass
NACA TN 1594, run 96 (air) 104.3 m/s 101.7 m/s pass, +2.6 %
run 60 (air) 100.0 m/s 103.0 m/s pass, −2.9 %
run 5 (Freon-12, ρ four times higher) 57.3 m/s 55.4 m/s pass, +3.4 %
Flutter frequency 24.6 / 24.8 / 27.2 Hz 22.1 / 22.0 / 25.2 Hz divergence +8–13 %
Frequencies: bending, second bending, torsion 6.65 / 41.6 / 48.6 Hz 6.25–6.45 / 35.8–39.2 / 44.6–47.6 Hz divergence +5–10 %
Cessna 172S, torsion box and strut are estimates no flutter up to 270 m/s, divergence ≥ 690 m/s regulations: none up to 1.2·V_D ≈ 112 m/s pass (plausibility)
NCAMP laminates, compressive modulus (3 layups) pass, 0.1–0.8 %
NCAMP laminates, tensile modulus (4 layups) 1 pass, 3 divergences +5–6 %
Tensile strength: 10/80/10 / 25/50/25 / 50/40/10 / [0/90] 463 / 879 / 1410 / 1287 MPa 462.5 / 717 / 1215 / 1166 MPa 1 pass, 3 divergences +10…+23 %
Compressive strength: 10/80/10 / 25/50/25 / 50/40/10 422 / 661 / 1016 MPa 465 / 600 / 835 MPa 1 pass, 2 divergences +10 and +22 %

Why it diverges

  • Flutter frequency. 8–13 % higher than the real one, even with four modes: the cause is strip theory (no tip losses), not the number of modes. NACA's 1949 calculation with the same theory gave the same error: 25.27 Hz vs. 22.1. The flutter speed still agrees.
  • Natural frequencies. The clamp in the model is perfectly rigid; the real one in the tunnel is more compliant.
  • Laminate strength is overestimated. A calculation based on the failure strain of a unidirectional ply (1.58 %) does not know that fibers in a laminate break earlier: a quasi-isotropic one fails at 1.25 %. This is a known effect: stress concentration at specimen edges, cracking of neighboring plies, interlaminar stresses at free edges. So the model rates parts with a layup as stronger than real ones — by up to 20 %. No correction factor was fitted.
  • Ply compression. NCAMP back-calculated the ply compressive strength from a cross-ply specimen using this same theory, so compression is not a fully independent check.

Limitations

  • Strip theory: no tip losses, no compressibility. Above M ≈ 0.5 the flutter speed is overestimated.
  • The strut is accounted for only in flutter: spar strength is still computed as for an equivalent cantilever.
  • Flutter of propeller blades and flapping wings is not computed: the oscillations there are of a different nature.
  • Wing-mounted masses (tanks, engines) are not included in flutter.
  • Nonlinear large-deflection flutter (as on the Pazy wing) is outside the model.

R22 in forward flight and autorotation: flapping blades, cyclic pitch, freewheel clutch (2026-11-23)

VALIDATE_ONLY=heli npm run physics -- --validate   # checks for this section (about 4 min)
npm run check   # everything together: 440 checks — 347 pass, 93 "DIVERGENCE", no failures

The last full run had one failure: translations of two new control labels were missing. They were added after the run; the translation check passes separately.

What was added to the core

  • Blades on flapping hinges (flapping on the rotor). This is how the R22 hub is built per the POH: teetering, with coning hinges.
    • Each blade's flapping has its own equation: Iβ·β̈ = M_aero + M_grav − Iβ·Ω²·(β₀ + β). Centrifugal force restores the blade at exactly once per revolution.
    • The blade stays a rigid body in Rapier. Flapping is superimposed on the position and velocity of the sections in the aerodynamics and loads, and the moment about the hinge is removed from the body — it is not transmitted to the hub.
    • Coning settles by itself: 1.8° in hover (the previous constant-coning estimate was 2°).
    • Blade loads include the blade's acceleration due to flapping (angular, centripetal, Coriolis).
  • Cyclic pitch (cyclic): blade angle += cos·cos ψ + sin·sin ψ by azimuth. The rotor axis for the flow is the normal to the tip-path plane.
  • Freewheel clutch (freewheel): the engine disengages; rpm is set by the flow and the rotor inertia. The tail rotor is driven by the main rotor and brakes it with its profile power.
    • The joint motor in Rapier cannot be switched off: with zero coefficients the joint becomes rigid. So the shaft joint is recreated without a motor.
  • Main rotor power is computed with sign. Coriolis forces rock the shaft twice per revolution, averaging zero. Taking only the positive part overestimates power fourfold. Tail rotor thrust is based on torque smoothed over 0.5 s.
  • Forward flight in a "tunnel" (src/cli/rotorflight.ts): the fuselage is free vertically, with flow from the front. Autopilot:
    • collective holds vertical speed, and in autorotation — rpm;
    • longitudinal cyclic balances drag;
    • lateral cyclic balances tail rotor thrust.

What the checks showed

Check Model Reference Result
90 kt level 96.6 hp 90 HP (Robinson, AAIB 11/98) pass, +7 %
60 kt, climb 1000 ft/min 108 hp 103 HP pass, +5 %
Autorotation 60 and 70 KIAS, 100 % 1317 and 1498 ft/min "usually less than 1500" (POH, SN-38) pass
Autorotation 75 KIAS, 90 % 1460 ft/min, glide ratio 5.2:1 about 1900 ft/min (glide ratio 4:1, POH) divergence −23 %
Minimum rate of descent at 90 % at 45 kt, the curve is flat: 1069–1101 ft/min at 40–53 kt 53 kt (Flight Training Guide) pass (45–60 kt)
R22 hover (earlier checks) 71.1 kW, as before unchanged

Info:

  • Blade flapping at 90 kt is ±5°, the tail rotor takes 6 hp.
  • Rotor rotational energy at 104 % is 298 HP·s, the margin down to 80 % is 122 HP·s. Robinson quotes 100 HP·s, but whether that is the total energy or the margin is unclear from the text.

Why it diverges and what is missing

  • Autorotation at 75 kt descends slower than the real one. At this speed about half the losses are fuselage drag (0.59 m², an estimate). The fuselage in the "tunnel" does not pitch, while the real one is nose-up in autorotation.

  • Blade strength in forward flight is info only; failure is disabled. The margin at the root drops to 0.8 at 90 kt. Reasons:

    • the spar is an equivalent box of 40 % chord; in the plane of rotation it is weaker than the real blade;
    • the hub suspension below the hinge, which on the R22 absorbs Coriolis forces, is not published and is not in the model.

    There are no blade load measurements, so there is nothing to fit.

  • There is no fuselage trim in pitch and roll, and no free flight of the helicopter in all degrees of freedom: fuselage angular rates do not enter the flapping equation. (Done on 2026-11-24 — see "R22 in free flight" at the top.)

  • Inflow through the disk is computed by annuli. There is no inflow skew across the disk in forward flight: the lateral flapping it causes is not reproduced.

  • There is no forward-flight program for the helicopter on the page yet — only the checks.

Why it diverges

  • Phugoid period. In the test the yoke was released and the elevator is free: it "floats", and the stability margin is smaller than with a fixed elevator. With a smaller margin the phugoid is longer. In addition, propeller slipstream over the tail is not accounted for.
  • Spiral. The model's lateral stability (C_lβ) is 1.4 times lower than computed, so bank from sideslip builds more slowly. How many degrees of rudder 2 cm of pedal gives is an estimate (≈ 3°): with 4° the model reaches 30° bank in 17 s. On the real aircraft the ailerons are free as well.
  • Directional stability C_nβ. It is higher than the NASA and JSBSim calculations. But a fin of 1.73 m² (Jane's) with "end-plate aspect ratio" and sidewash per the DATCOM breakdown gives 0.1–0.15. The propeller normal force in sideslip, which reduces directional stability, is not computed in the model.

Limitations

  • Free (floating) control surface: control surface hinge moments are not modeled — a surface stays where it was set.
  • The propeller slipstream does not blow over the tail and fuselage. Slipstream swirl, oblique inflow to the propeller and P-factor are not accounted for.
  • At large deflections control surfaces are linear: separation from the deflected part is not accounted for.
  • The wake behind the wing is straight, streamwise: downwash does not deflect it and it does not roll up gradually.
  • The takeoff roll is in a plane: the wheels are not steered on the runway.

Cessna 172S fixed-pitch propeller: engine–propeller rpm equilibrium (2026-11-12)

VALIDATE_ONLY=cessna npm run physics -- --validate   # Cessna section only, about 3 min
npm run check   # (as of 2026-11-12) full run after all three improvements: 346 checks — 284 pass, 62 "DIVERGENCE", no failures

A continuation of the fifth review: the largest divergence there was the Cessna climb (+49 % at sea level, +60 % at 8000 ft). The cause was known: the propeller in the model is a momentum disk with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller has no set rpm. The rpm settles where engine torque equals the torque the propeller absorbs. At low speed the propeller is "heavier", rpm is below 2700, and the engine delivers less power. The rule is the same: the references are only independent 172S POH data (data/research.md, part 4.2), nothing was tuned to fit them.

What was done in the core

  • src/core/propeller.ts (new) — a blade element propeller model with momentum theory on each annulus: axial and tangential induced velocities, Prandtl tip and root losses. At each radius a single equation is solved for the inflow angle φ (the Ning 2014 formulation, written for a propeller): Ωr·(sin²φ − σ'·Cn/4F) − V·(sin φ·cos φ + σ'·Ct/4F) = 0. There is no singularity at V = 0; the root is found by bisection. Section coefficients come from the shared airfoilCoeffs model (full range of angles, Prandtl–Glauert, compressibility drag rise from the sixth review). There is propellerEquilibrium — the equilibrium rpm for a given engine torque.
  • src/core/sim.ts — the propeller drive has an optional fixedPitch block. If it is set, rpm is a state variable: I·dΩ/dt = Q_engine − Q_prop. Engine torque = throttle × power/ω_rated × altitude lapse. Without the block everything is as before (a disk with an efficiency — like a constant-speed propeller; projects from design.ts are built this way). At zero throttle the propeller windmills and brakes the aircraft. Sample has propRpm, propEfficiency.
  • IO-360-L2A engine. At full throttle torque is constant and power is proportional to rpm. The basis is type certificate EASA.IM.E.032 (Issue 03, 2022, sec. 6 "Ratings", full throttle at sea level): 119 kW (160 hp) at 2400 rpm and 134 kW (180 hp) at 2700 rpm. That is 474 N·m at both points, to within 0.1 % (data/research.md, 4.2, item 7). Below 2400 rpm there are no data points; constant torque there is an assumption. New field powerplant.ratedRpm = 2700.
  • Flight program (programs.ts). At full throttle in level flight at sea level the fixed-pitch propeller would spin the engine up to 3080 rpm. So the program, like a pilot, pulls back the throttle and holds no more than ratedRpm: the 2700 redline (POH, section 2). Maximum speed is now under this limit, which is how the POH defines its 126 kt. New fields in the flight results: vMaxRpm, cruiseRpm, cruisePropEfficiency, climbRpm, climbPropEfficiency. No other aircraft have fixedPitch; nothing changed for them.

McCauley 1A170E/JHA7660 propeller (src/presets/cessna172.ts): 2 blades, D = 76 in (POH), pitch 60 in — from the designation "7660". McCauley measures pitch at 0.75R. What this means

  • Climb: the divergence shrank from +49…+60 % to +17…+18 %. It remains for three reasons, each pushing the same way.
    1. The model propeller is "light": at the same speed and rpm it absorbs 10–23 % less power than the real one, most of all at low J. Climb rpm is therefore higher than it would be with the real propeller, and the engine delivers more power.
    2. Propeller efficiency in the climb is 0.68–0.71. Estimates from the POH put the real one at about 0.6–0.65. The model lacks flow blockage by the cowling and the increase in fuselage drag in the propeller slipstream.
    3. The model airframe needs less power than the real one: the parasite drag area of 0.36 m² is an estimate.
  • The "light" propeller is probably the geometry. The blade angle is known only through the 60 in pitch. What it is measured from (the flat side or the chord) and where the airfoil's zero lift lies are estimates. At J ≈ 0.7 the sections operate at an angle of attack of about 1°, and a 1° error changes absorbed power by about 15 %. For the static case, the sensitivity is printed in the divergence reason: with chord ×1.25 (AF 100, also a typical value) it would be 2315 rpm, with c_l,max 1.6 — 2192. I did not change the chord: that would be fitting to the number being checked. There is also a sign that it is not only the geometry: the APC 9x4.7 SF propeller, built from UIUC measured geometry, also falls short on C_T and C_P by 20–26 % in static conditions (the "small propeller" section). Outside the experiment I ran the same APC through the new solver: C_T 0.095, C_P 0.036, FM 0.651. The previous model of blades as Rapier bodies gave 0.644 — two different implementations agree.

  • Cruise power is now 3 % further below the POH than before. Previously the disk efficiency (0.85 of ideal, about 0.80) happened to be close to the real one. Now the isolated model propeller efficiency in cruise is 0.82–0.85: there are no losses from the cowling and from the slipstream on the fuselage. So the earlier "on average −6.5 %" partly rested on an underestimated propeller efficiency.
  • Verdicts. The overloaded Cessna is still "Does not fly". The model's climb is still optimistic, but roughly three times less so than before. Maximum speed is now limited by 2700 rpm and has become 7 % lower than before.

  • Measured geometry of the McCauley 1A170E blade (blade angle and chord along the radius, airfoil) or a wind-tunnel test of this propeller. Without them the "lightness" cannot be split between geometry and the section model.
  • Stall delay on a rotating blade (Snel, Du–Selig) and gradual stall beyond c_l,max. This affects the static case and low J, and the small APC propeller awaits the same corrections.
  • Flow blockage ahead of the propeller by the cowling and hub, the increase in fuselage drag in the slipstream.
  • Blade thickness along the radius (currently 0.09 along the whole length).
  • Propeller reaction torque and gyroscopic moment on the airframe are not modelled, as before.
  • A fixed-pitch propeller for projects from the builder (design.ts): they still use a disk. An estimate of geometry from diameter and power is needed.

Experiment: at A0 ≈ 15° and k ≈ 0.1 the peak C_L of 2.1–2.3 hardly depends on Re (0.5–3.6·10⁶), even though the static c_l,max rises from 1.0 to 1.4. This is the dynamic stall vortex: lift holds and grows beyond static stall until the leading-edge vortex passes off the trailing edge.

What was changed in the core

src/core/aero.ts, dynamicStall: a vortex following the Beddoes–Leishman scheme was added to the pressure lag (Tp) and separation lag (Tf). The vorticity C_V is the difference between the attached-flow normal force and the force with lagged separation (in the scheme C_N^C·(1 − K_N)); its increments feed into the vortex normal force with lag Tv while the vortex is over the airfoil (τ_v ≤ Tvl from stall onset by the criterion). Then the vortex force decays with Tv/2; if stall continues, after Tvl + Tsh the next vortex begins (Tsh = 2(1 − w)/St). Stall onset is the lagged angle beyond the static stall angle, i.e. C_N1 is the static stall normal force. The constants are the published ones for NACA 0012, not tuned to the references: Tp 1.7, Tf 3.0, Tv 6.0 (Leishman & Beddoes; the same numbers are the OpenFAST AeroDyn defaults), Tvl 7.0 (Leishman & Beddoes 1986 for NACA 0012 at M 0.3; the OpenFAST default is 11), St 0.19. Not introduced: the Tf and Tv corrections by cycle stage (multipliers 0.25…4 in OpenFAST), the vortex suction force and pitching moment. It acts only on parts with unsteady flow — that is, flapping wings; propellers, airplanes and helicopters are not affected.

Also checked with Tvl = 11 (OpenFAST): the peak C_L is the same, only the post-peak decay changes.

Sixth physics check: blade-tip compressibility and coaxial rotors (2026-11-12)

A continuation of the fifth check (section below): two hover divergences from measurements — the R22 hovered on 12 % less power than per the POH, and the Harrington coaxial rotor took 14–26 % more power than in the model. Same rule: the reference is a measurement, parameters are not tuned to the aircraft being checked. Sources and digitization — data/research.md, section 4.6.

npm run check (together with work from neighbouring sessions — the Cessna propeller and dynamic stall): 346 checks, 284 pass, 62 "DIVERGENCE", no failures; 63 lines for information.

Compressibility drag rise (src/core/aero.ts)

Previously compressibility in the model changed only the c_l slope (Prandtl–Glauert). Now wave drag per Lock is added to the attached-flow c_d, with the drag-divergence Mach number in Korn's form:

M_dd = κ_A − t/c − s·|c_l|,   M_cr = M_dd − (0.1/80)^⅓,   Δc_d = 20·(M − M_cr)⁴ for M > M_cr

The coefficients were taken from a measurement of the airfoil itself, not of a rotor: two-dimensional NACA 0012 in the Langley LTPT tunnel (Carpenter, NACA TN 4357, fig. 5). M_dd (where dc_d/dM = 0.1) at α = 0, 4, 6, 8° fell on the line 0.800 − 0.31·c_l with a scatter of ±0.02, i.e. κ_A = 0.92, s = 0.31. Korn's classic s = 0.1 is for airfoils at their design c_l; for a loaded NACA 0012 M_dd drops three times faster (with that s, Korn–Lock at α = 4–8° gave almost no rise where c_d had already doubled in the experiment). The −t/c term is confirmed by the text of the same report: a blade with an NACA 0015 tip diverges at a c̄_l 0.10 lower than NACA 0012, and 0.03 of thickness = 0.31 × 0.10.

6-series airfoils behave differently: their nose suction peak is smaller, and M_dd depends weakly on c_l. With the NACA 0012 numbers, a rotor with the R22 airfoil (NACA 63₂-015, Shivers & Carpenter, NACA TN 3850) got a power rise of +45 % at M_t 0.71, while in the experiment it was only +4.4 %. Therefore the airfoil got an optional dragRise field. For the R22 it holds Korn's original numbers for 6-series airfoils (κ_A = 0.87, s = 0.1; W. H. Mason, "Some Transonic Aerodynamics", p. 51, and "Configuration Aerodynamics", ch. 7; Mason's text was not accessed, the values are from two secondary accounts) — these are published values, not tuned ones. By default (all other airfoils) — the NACA 0012 numbers.

κ_int of coaxial rotors (src/core/design.ts): 1.16 → 1.28

Primary source — Leishman and Syal's work (JAHS 2008; derivations and figures are in Syal's master's thesis, UMD 2008, which is downloadable). There κ_int is the ratio of the induced power of the pair to two isolated rotors at the same disk loading, i.e. the same definition as in the model. Momentum theory gives 1.281 if the lower rotor is in the fully contracted wake of the upper one: this is the lowest possible value. If the rotors are in the same plane — 1.414. For both Harrington rotors Leishman and Syal use 1.28. An independent measurement — Cameron, Karpatne, Sirohi (J. Aircraft 2016): upper rotor +18 %, lower +49 %, 1.33 on average. The value 1.16 (from a forum) is below the theoretical minimum; it was not found in the primary sources.

Found and fixed

  1. The coaxial rotor rig assembled the upper rotor incorrectly (hoverRig in validation.ts, a bug from the fifth check). For the mirrored blade (clockwise rotor) the root was placed on the other side of the axis, and the blade went through the axis. Such a rotor produced 4.5 times less thrust. The fifth check compared the experiment against a pair in which mostly one rotor was producing thrust. With the fixed rig and the old κ_int = 1.16, Harrington rotor 1 gives −7…−14 % instead of −14…−26 %: at low thrust the rig bug was the main cause, at high thrust — κ_int. The helicopter builder (design.ts) and the quadcopter preset place the blade correctly; the bug did not affect them.
  2. No wave drag — added (above).
  3. κ_int = 1.16 — replaced with 1.28 (above).

R22: compressibility is not the main cause. According to measurements on a rotor with the same airfoil (TN 3850), the compressibility power rise at M_t 0.71 is only 4.4 %, and the R22 has M_t 0.60–0.67 (104 % rpm, −20…+40 °C) — even less. In the model it added about 1 % to the R22 (−20 °C: −12.0 → −11.1 %). The model even computes the rotor itself 5 % more expensive than the experiment (the same TN 3850 at low M_t). So the 11–13 % lies outside blade aerodynamics: the downwash load on the cabin (2–5 % of thrust) is not accounted for; the tail rotor and transmission share (15 %) is an estimate; interpreting the steep portion of the POH chart as the takeoff 131 BHP is also an estimate. None of these numbers was tuned to the POH.

While only the 0012 airfoil was being checked, with it the R22 at −20 °C (M_t 0.667) got +18 % power, and at +20 °C — +2 %. Such a spread is a sign that the 0012 coefficients do not carry over to the 6-series. That is why the separate TN 3850 rotor was needed as an independent check.

The RMS error of the coaxial pair over six points of the two rotors is 5.6 % with κ_int = 1.28 and 9.9 % with 1.16. The residual is in the slope: in the experiment the "pair / two isolated rotors" ratio grows with thrust (rotor 1: 1.22 → 1.37, rotor 2: 1.09 → 1.28), while the model's κ_int is constant. Therefore at low thrust the model overestimates the pair's power, and at high thrust underestimates it.

What changed for the aircraft

  • Coaxial helicopters (Ka-26, Ka-32, designs from the builder): the pair's induced power increased by a factor of 1.28/1.16 = 1.10, hover power — by about 8 % (Ka-26 design: 473 kW, mutual interference ×1.194 instead of ×1.10). The Ka-32 still "Flies" (2310 of 3266 kW).
  • Main rotors at M_t > 0.6 (R22 and any fast rotors): profile power increases at the blade tips.
  • Airplane propellers: blade tips at M 0.75–0.9 get wave drag (applies to the blade-element propeller model; not to the actuator-disk propeller with constant efficiency).
  • Airplane wings, ornithopters and small rotors (M < 0.5): unchanged. Δc_d is computed from the stall-limited C_L, so there is no spurious rise beyond stall or at low M.

What remains

  • The drag rise beyond M_dd per Lock (fourth power) is gentler than the two-dimensional experiment and steeper than the blade-tip experiment. There is no correction for three-dimensional tip flow (because of this FM at M_t 0.70 is 5 % below the experiment).
  • There are two airfoil families: NACA 4-digit (the default, from the 0012 tunnel test) and the 6-series (Korn's numbers). For 5-digit airfoils (23015 — in TN 3850 it diverges earlier than 63₂-015), low-Reynolds-number airfoils and supercritical airfoils there are no specific numbers. The text-description project builder gives all airfoils the default values.
  • The R22 is still 9–13 % below the POH. Candidates: the downwash load on the cabin, tail rotor power (a measurement or calculation of the R22 tail rotor is needed), the interpretation of the POH chart.
  • κ_int is constant, whereas in the experiment mutual interference grows with thrust; Leishman's textbook (PHA) was never accessed.

Fifth physics check: comparison with real measurements (2026-11-12)

npm run physics -- --validate   # only the comparisons with measurements, a few minutes
npm run check                   # everything together: 286 checks — 258 pass, 28 "DIVERGENCE", no failures; 23 lines INFO

The rule for this check is the user's own words: "tests must not be tuned to pass. Physics must be checked with maximum realism." The previous four passes compared the model mostly against formulas. Here the references are measurements: airfoil wind-tunnel tests, propeller and rotor test-stand data, tables from pilot's operating handbooks. Numbers and source links are in data/research.md, part 4. The checks are in src/cli/validation.ts.

The checks gained two new outcomes (src/cli/physics.ts, makeReporter):

  • DIVERGENCE — the model missed the measurement by more than a tolerance justified by the reference's uncertainty and the known simplifications of the model. It is printed with the reason and counted on a separate line in the summary. It does not fail the run, but it is not hidden either.
  • INFO — the number is printed but does not count as a check. This covers comparisons with a reference that a model parameter was tuned to, and comparisons with a quantity that is not a reference.

The tolerance of each comparison is broken down in the code: what it is made of and how much each part contributes. No tolerance was tuned to the result. Where the budget came out smaller than the discrepancy, the result is "DIVERGENCE", not a widened tolerance.

What this means for the verdicts

  • Cessna. The model describes steady flight within 4–9 % in power, and stall accurately. Climb is strongly overestimated (+50–60 %): in the model the propeller is a disc with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller at low speed turns below 2700 rpm, with an efficiency of about 0.6. The "Does not fly" verdicts for an overloaded aircraft are therefore optimistic: the model may pass an aircraft that in reality will not climb.
  • Rotors in hover. The model with κ = 1.15 correctly describes a twisted rotor (Carpenter, within 5 %) and the Harrington single rotor. For an untwisted rotor and at low Reynolds numbers (TN 626) it underestimates power by 4–11 %. For the real R22 the discrepancy is 12 %. Known causes: no compressibility drag rise at the blade tip (M 0.62–0.65; for the Carpenter rotor at M 0.7 FM is 10 % lower than at M 0.3), no download from the wake on the cabin (2–5 % of thrust), the tail rotor and transmission share of 15 % is an estimate. The model R22 hovers where the real one no longer can: its hover ceiling is optimistic by roughly 2000–2500 ft.
  • Coaxial rotors (outdated — see the sixth check: κ_int = 1.28, and the coaxial rotor test stand had been assembled with an error). κ_int = 1.16 was taken from a forum; the primary source was not read. Harrington's experiment shows that a coaxial pair takes 1.22–1.37 times more power than two separate rotors at half thrust each, while the model gives about 1.12. The hover power of the Ka-26 and Ka-32 in the model is probably underestimated by 10–20 %. The value 1.16 was not changed: there is no reliable number to replace it (in Harrington's data the split into profile and induced parts is unstable, rotor 1 is wooden, with very low solidity). A comparison with Harrington's second rotor and with the primary source is needed.
  • Post-stall (the "Dune" ornithopter, blades in reverse flow) the model underestimates aerodynamic forces at 30–60° by 10–20 %.
  • Flapping-wing aircraft. The model describes SmartBird's shaft power within the accuracy of the paper. Snowbird with the real kinematics does not stay airborne in the model: thrust is a third of drag, and gliding drag is 22 % less than measured. On the real wing the tip operates at ±20–23° — in the dynamic-stall regime, where lift is sustained by the leading-edge stall vortex. The model did not have this vortex; it does now, but the discrepancy remains (see "Seventh physics check"). The verdict for large slow flapping-wing aircraft ("Does not fly") is therefore pessimistic.

Found and fixed

  1. Cruise power was taken before the flight condition had settled (programs.ts, flight program). Power was averaged over 22–30 s after leaving the maximum speed. The speed controller (0.08 per m/s) was still oscillating by then, with a period of about 40 s. At 112 knots at 8000 ft it gave 78 kW instead of the steady-state 76, and at neighbouring speeds the curve jumped. Now the cruise controller is damped (0.25 per m/s), and power is taken only when for 16 s in a row the speed stays within 0.2 m/s, altitude does not change and throttle does not wander. If it has not settled within 200 s, the report says so. The old comparison at 124 knots: was 96.3 kW, now 93.7 kW.
  2. New flight program mode — steady climb at a given speed at full throttle (climbSpeed): rate of climb. Needed for the comparison with the POH.
  3. The altitude controller of the "Takeoff and hover" program oscillated at low density. For the R22 at 1524 m altitude wandered by ±3 m with a period of about 9 s, the hover was not counted, and the mean power was biased. The old "R22 at 5000 ft" comparison (85.3 kW) relied on this. The inner loop (collective → acceleration) is slower at low density, and the outer one was too stiff. The altitude and speed gains of 1.0 and 1.8 were replaced with 0.4 and 1.2. Oscillation for the R22: at sea level 1.2 → 0.55 m, at 1524 m 6.2 → 1.9 m (hover counted), at 3000 m 3.5 → 1.7 m; for the quadcopter and Ka-26 no worse than before. For comparisons with the POH, hover is still computed on a fixed body, with the collective pitch trimmed for thrust equal to weight.
  4. Flapping-wing references switched from tuned numbers to published ones (src/presets/flappers.ts):
    • Snowbird: frequency 0.83 → 0.65 Hz (dissertation, "observed in flight"; 0.83 was a paraphrase of "16 flaps in 19.3 s"); flap amplitude — by tip travel ±1.0 m instead of the tuned ±4°; twist ±45° → ±7° (structural limit); only the panels from 6 m flap, the inner part is fixed — as on the real aircraft (bracing wires at 6 m); masses — from the dissertation's mass table (wing 27.6 kg); c_l,max 1.5 → 1.55 (DT-HPO1 airfoil with early transition).
    • SmartBird: drive efficiency 0.6 (estimate) → 0.34 (measured in the same paper). The Snowbird verdict changed: "Flies at the limit" → "Does not fly" (thrust is a third of drag). This is not an input error: the model with the real kinematics does not reproduce the real flight, and the old verdict relied on tuned amplitude and twist. SmartBird still "Flies"; electrical power at 5 m/s is 15.7 W (per the paper, 23 W at the design condition, of which about 5 W are servos).

Page freezes on heavy vehicles (2026-11-11)

Complaint: "I increased the number of main rotors — and everything froze." There were four causes; all are fixed.

  1. Frame computation was not time-limited. Twelve rotors means 37 bodies; 0.05 s of model time took 0.5 s to compute. After a slow frame the page asked to compute even more (the time step grows with the delay), and the display went into a "spin": half-second frames, buttons not responding. Now computation gets no more than 20 ms per frame. A heavy vehicle runs slower than the selected pace, and the line under the picture says so: "computation cannot keep up… display is running N times slower than selected". "To result" also computes in time-based chunks rather than in 0.02 s of model time.
  2. The sliders for the number of rotors, blades, wings and seats were fractional — one could set 4.04 rotors (the builder turned this into five hubs, two of them almost at the same point). Now the step is 1 with integer limits, and a fractional value from an old link is rejected with an explanation.
  3. Nothing prevented placing rotors so that their discs overlap. Multicopter rotors are placed in a circle, with 2·L·sin(π/N) between adjacent axes; if this is less than the diameter (with a 5 % tolerance), the design is rejected: "12 rotors of radius 0.12 m on a 0.35 m arm do not fit… Increase the arm or reduce the radius".

Measured on the page, with 0.05 s of model time requested per frame: before (twelve rotors) a frame took 0.5 s; now (eight rotors) — 23–27 ms, computing as much as fits. At a 10× slowdown such a vehicle keeps up fully (14 ms per frame).

  1. "Freeze" after a rejected design (second complaint, a coaxial Ka-52 with the rotor-count slider at 4). The page was not frozen: the design with four rotors on one axis was rejected, there was no model, and the stand showed the frozen picture of the previous vehicle, said "Ready to launch", and "Launch" did nothing. The reason was only at the bottom of the assumptions screen. Now the stand removes the picture, says "Model not built" with the reason and a "← To assumptions" button, and "Launch" and "To result" are disabled. The message is clearer: "4 rotors on one axis cannot be built — only a coaxial pair is arranged that way… Three or more rotors are placed in a circle: set the arm to at least the radius". What remains: computation of heavy vehicles itself has not been sped up — eight to twelve rotors run 5–10 times slower than real time, and "To result" takes minutes for them. The page stays responsive meanwhile.

Coaxial helicopter and a test on a real AI (2026-11-11)

Coaxial layout

A helicopter design with two rotors and zero arm (rotor.rotorCount = 2, rotor.armLength = 0) is built as coaxial (src/core/design.ts): two hubs on a common axis, separated vertically by 0.2 radius; the rotors counter-rotate and are controlled by collective pitch. Previously such a design was rejected: "rotors overlap".

Coaxial rotors interfere with each other — the lower one works in the wake of the upper one. The induced power of the pair is higher than that of two identical isolated rotors by a factor of κ_int. In the model κ_int = 1.16 (from measurements; simple momentum theory gives 1.28–1.41; sources in data/research.md). With 1.28 the hover power would be about 7 % higher.

The Ka-26 reference design (src/presets/designs.ts; rotor span, mass and power from open data; chord, rpm, blade mass and spar web are estimates): "Flies", hover 438 kW of 478 kW, safety margin 2.0. The hand estimate of power is 429 kW (2 % divergence). Rotor interference adds 10 % to hover power.

What the live test found

None of these errors were caught by the checks without the AI.

  1. Generation from a description did not work at all. With two new fields the design schema became too large: the AI responded with the error "compiled grammar is too large". The schema was simplified: coaxiality is determined by the number of rotors and zero arm, without a separate field; wing mass "compute from material" is 0 instead of null.
  2. The wind-tunnel autopilot could not balance lift against weight on a fast vehicle. For the "seagull" at 10 m/s lift changes by 0.49 of weight per degree, while the autopilot allowed a slope of no more than 0.25 (tuned for SmartBird and Snowbird) and oscillated between two angles. A stalled regime was chosen, power came out at 86 W, and the wing "broke". Now the slope is taken from lifting-line theory, and once angles with a lift deficit and a lift excess are found, the angle is searched between them. SmartBird did not change; Snowbird shifted within 1.5 % (in the tunnel 866 W without energy recovery and 314 W with recovery instead of 868 and 316).
  3. After breakage the computation diverged: the Mach number of the debris reached 10¹⁹. For a detached light part the added air mass is larger than its own, and computation from the previous step's acceleration is unstable. Now added mass is not computed for debris, the Mach number is taken only over intact parts, and free flight is terminated after breakage.
  4. The "bird" spar was wider than that of the references and previously lost stability. Now the section is the same as for SmartBird and Snowbird.
  5. The Ka-32 blade "broke" on the ground under its own weight (at 0.017 s): it was treated as a hollow thin-walled box. Rotor blades have honeycomb or foam filler behind the spar, and the walls are stiffened. The structure gained a structure.filled flag: local buckling is not checked for such a section; the other failure modes are checked as usual. It is set on the blades of helicopters built from a description and on the R22 reference (its result did not change).
  6. An old builder error: for a clockwise-rotating rotor with three or more blades, the blade rotation angle went past 360°, and the design was rejected. This also affected multicopters with three-blade rotors.

Unresolved

The first two items were resolved by the fourth physics review (section "Fourth physics review" above): the shear came from resolving loads along the part's axes instead of the axis of the coned blade; the resonance warning came from the absence of aerodynamic flap damping. The text below is left as originally written.

  • The AI-built Ka-32 gets "Breaks up", and this is an error of the model, not of the vehicle. Without strength taken into account it hovers: 2,119 kW of 3,266 kW. The blade breaks by web shear (margin about 1). The spar web is treated as unidirectional fibreglass, whose shear strength is 40 MPa; in real blades shear is carried by ±45° plies. A laminate web model is needed — it will also make buckling more accurate. The Ka-26 reference has enough margin only with a 9 mm web.
  • The "close to resonance" warning on blades. The first flap frequency of a blade rigidly fixed in the hub is always about 1.1 per rev; in real blades flapping is strongly damped by the air, while the model has 3 % damping.

Ornithopter free flight (2026-11-11)

The Snowbird numbers in this and the following sections predate the fifth physics check. With the kinematics from Reichert's thesis (0.65 Hz, tip stroke ±1.0 m, twist ±7°) the Snowbird model does not stay in the air — see "Fifth physics check".

npm run stand -- smartbird free    # trim search in the stream, then free flight
npm run report -- snowbird free

The new free program is "Ornithopter free flight" (src/core/programs.ts). On the page it is the default for SmartBird and Snowbird.

  1. Trim search — the same wind-tunnel autopilot: the body is fixed in the oncoming flow, and the wing incidence and twist are tuned. On the page this part runs accelerated (1–5 s).
  2. Release. The oncoming flow is converted into the vehicle's velocity: velocity V is added to every body, and to the wind as well (Sim.boost). The flow around the vehicle does not change. The body is released: forward and vertical motion are free, heading and body pitch are held.
  3. Flight — 16 flaps, but no less than 8 s. Once per flap the autopilot corrects the wing incidence (altitude) and the twist (speed).

How the autopilot works. A wing damps its own sink: as it descends, it meets the flow at a higher angle. So over a flap what settles is not an acceleration but a sink rate proportional to the deviation of the incidence from the trim value: v_y = V·Δθ. On each flap the autopilot refines the trim incidence and adds a correction that removes 35% of the altitude error per flap. Speed is handled the same way, through twist. The first version of the autopilot assumed the angle sets acceleration and held neither altitude nor speed: SmartBird lost 0.43 m and 5% of its speed in 8 s.

The measure of flight is total energy (altitude + V²/2g): its loss over the distance flown equals the thrust deficit. A loss above 20% of drag is "Does not fly", 5 to 20% is "Flies at the limit". Power is compared with the available power the same way as in the wind tunnel.

Limitations:

  • Heading, roll and body pitch are held perfectly: the tail surfaces and lateral motion are not modelled. Since 2026-11-12 the moment used to hold the body is measured and named in the verdict (see "Fourth physics check").

Strength check (2026-11-11)

npm run physics -- --strength   # strength checks only, a few seconds

The strength calculation (src/core/strength.ts, src/core/section.ts, loads — src/core/sim.ts) was verified against strength-of-materials formulas on individual sections and on a wing in a flow: 25 checks, all pass.

What was verified Discrepancy
Box area and moment of inertia, bending stress, torsion (Bredt), shear, equivalent stress (von Mises), margin to rounding
Critical wall stress: compression, flapwise bending, in-plane (chordwise) bending to rounding
Tube: bending in two planes to rounding
Fatigue: Basquin curve, Goodman correction up to 0.1%
Wing in steady flow: root stresses from lift and drag 0.5%
Elastic wing near resonance (drive at half the natural frequency): stress range × 1.33 0.2%

Four bugs were found and fixed:

  1. Composite walls buckled "like metal". The critical stress was computed with the formula for an isotropic plate using the longitudinal modulus. In a composite the wall is also held by the transverse modulus, which is several times lower. Now the plate stiffness is B = √(Q₁₁·Q₂₂) + Q₁₂ + 2·Q₆₆, σ_cr = k/4 · π²t²/(6w²) · B. For unidirectional carbon fibre (135 / 10 / 5 GPa) B = 50 GPa instead of 297 GPa — 5.9 times less. For metal the formula reduces to the previous one. The transverse modulus and shear modulus were added to the library for the carbon fibres, glass fibre, aramid and spruce; where no data exist, they are taken from a generic carbon fibre and marked as estimates.
  2. One critical stress for the whole section. The lower of two was taken (flange in compression, web in flapwise bending) and compared with the highest compression at any corner. Now each of the four box walls is checked separately: its own width, its own stress distribution, coefficient k from 4 (uniform compression) to 23.9 (bending in the plane of the wall) per EN 1993-1-5, Table 4.1.
  3. For the tube, bending in two planes was added arithmetically — the stress was overestimated by up to √2 times. Now it uses the resultant moment.
  4. Fatigue was computed only for the upper flange, without in-plane bending. Now it uses the worst of the four corners of the section.

The Snowbird spar in the model was a guess: a unidirectional carbon-fibre box with a 4 mm wall. It would weigh 43 kg per wing — as much as the whole vehicle. The design of the real spar has not been published, and its wing is supported by drive cables, which are not in the model. Fitting the guess to the answer would be dishonest, so the Snowbird's structural members were removed: strength is not checked, and this is stated in the vehicle's description.

Along the way a report flaw was found: the warning "Strength not checked" was printed only with the verdict "Flies". Now it appears with any verdict, and the report telemetry has the line "Strength margin: not checked".

Caveats:

  • Walls are treated as unidirectional, fibres along the span. Real spars have ±45° plies in the webs, which are more stable. For a library material the estimate is correct; for a real structure it is conservative.
  • Not computed: shear buckling of the walls, composite delamination, global buckling of the wing, stress concentration at the attachment fittings.
  • Fatigue is computed only for materials with data (metals); there are no data for composites.

Unsteady flow over a flapping wing (2026-11-11)

npm run physics -- --unsteady   # unsteady-model checks only, a few seconds

For a surface with aero.unsteady: true (SmartBird and Snowbird) lift is computed with flow memory (src/core/aero.ts, src/core/sim.ts):

  1. Lift lag — the Wagner function in Jones's approximation, φ(s) = 1 − 0.165·e^(−0.0455·s) − 0.335·e^(−0.3·s), s — distance in semichords. The angle of attack is taken from the downwash at the ¾-chord point (including the section's pitch rate). The force is perpendicular to the effective flow: when it lags, it is tilted backwards and the stroke thrust is lower.
  2. Stall lag — a simplified Beddoes–Leishman model (trailing-edge separation): two first-order lags, Tp = 1.7 and Tf = 3.0 semichords. The constants are taken from the literature for the NACA 0012 airfoil and were not tuned. With a rapid increase in angle, lift exceeds the static maximum.
  3. Added mass — both from flapping and from the section's rotation in the flow.

Caveats:

  • Snowbird's stroke amplitude has not been published and is tuned so that the work per flap matches the pilot's estimate (600–700 W on the power stroke). With the new model this is ±4° (628 W) instead of ±3°; the twist limit has been raised to ±45° — above the flow angle at the tip.
  • SmartBird's power is now 32% below the published figure (was 17%): within the spec tolerance (40%), but worse.
  • The flow "remembers" the past, so after each settings change the wind-tunnel autopilot skips a flap cycle and shifts the controls smoothly. The trim search takes 60–110 cycles (for Snowbird, 137 s of model time, 3–4 s of computation).
  • Not taken into account: the dynamic-stall vortex, loss of leading-edge suction on thin airfoils at low Reynolds numbers, spanwise unsteadiness. The verdict warns about this.
  • The ornithopter from "Dune" and vehicles built from a description are still computed quasi-steadily: they flap in place, without oncoming flow, and the wing is in deep stall.

What was found and fixed:

  1. The wind-tunnel autopilot got stuck. Thrust depends non-monotonically on wing twist: too little and the wing stalls, too much and it "feathers" and produces no thrust. The old controller turned the twist "in one direction only", considered balance reached with a thrust shortfall of up to 1 % of weight (while the verdict required strictly ≥ 0), and did not allow the incidence angle above the stall angle. Because of this SmartBird "did not hold its weight" and Snowbird "did not pull". Now the twist is swept over the whole range, lift is balanced by the secant method, the T = D regime is searched for on the unstalled branch, and strength and peaks are computed only at the regime found (parts do not break during the search trials).
  2. Flapping power was overstated by a factor of two. It was computed as a sum of absolute values: braking the wing cost as much as accelerating it. An actuator that brakes a part spends no energy. Now there are two quantities: without recovery of braking energy (sum of the positive parts over the actuators) and with full recovery (signed average over whole cycles — the work done on the air). For the "Dune" ornithopter these are 7,630 and 2,890 MW instead of 12,400 MW. The label "with full recovery" was previously attached to a number that was not that.
  3. Averages over an incomplete cycle. Power and lift were averaged over windows of 1 s and 0.5 s — for slow flapping (Snowbird, 0.83 Hz) that is not a whole cycle. Now the windows are multiples of the cycle.
  4. Snowbird data were guesses even though they are published (data/research.md): wing area 29.2 m² (was 39 m² "so that it holds its weight"), flight mass 114.3 kg, 16 flaps in 19.3 s = 0.83 Hz (was 0.6), pilot power 600–700 W on the power stroke (was 300 W). With the real area the aircraft flies at C_L = 1.24 — right at the stall.
  5. SmartBird drag was tuned to the published lift-to-drag ratio L/D ≈ 7 (was ~10).

What came out after the fixes:

These are results of the quasi-steady model; after accounting for unsteadiness the numbers are different — see the section above.

  • SmartBird — "Flies": thrust margin 2–6 % of weight, 10.7 W for flapping without energy recovery (6.8 W with recovery) versus 13 W per the paper (level flight at 4.7 m/s without servos; 18 W with them): −17 %.
  • Snowbird — "Flies at the limit", as the spec requires: thrust is short by 3.8 N (9 % of drag, 0.34 % of weight), power suffices only with energy recovery (309 W; without recovery 700 W against 650 W). In the record of the real flight total energy and speed were also slowly decreasing. Caveat: the flapping amplitude is not published and was chosen (±3°) so that the work per flap matches the pilot's estimate; the power check is therefore not independent.

New verdict rules for flapping flight:

  • A thrust shortfall of less than 20 % of drag (the spec's tolerance for reference aircraft) is "at the limit", not "does not fly": the model does not know drag more precisely than that.
  • If power suffices only with recovery of the wings' braking energy — "at the limit" with an explanation; if it is insufficient even with recovery — "does not fly".
  • Unsteadiness warning: at a reduced frequency k ≥ 0.1 the steady-flow model overstates flapping thrust — by Theodorsen–Garrick theory for an airfoil, by a factor of 2.1–2.2 at k ≈ 0.3. For SmartBird and Snowbird unsteadiness is now taken into account (section above); the warning remains for surfaces without unsteady.

Known numerical errors (not fixed, covered by checks):

  • The velocity-driven actuator falls short of the amplitude by about 1 % at 120 steps per cycle and by about 3 % in power at 40 steps per cycle (ornithopter); it goes away as the time step decreases.
  • The engine computes in single precision: the centre of mass of an ornithopter in vacuum drifts by 5.6 mm in 3.5 s with a fuselage travel of ±515 mm (1 %); the error grows as the time step decreases — this is rounding, not integration.

Stage 6: publication

cp .env.example .env        # AI key, monitoring password, salt, limits
npm run build               # build the page into dist/
npm run serve               # the whole service: page, API, storage — http://localhost:8139

The service is a single Node process (src/server/server.ts → src/server/app.ts):

  • Reports via permanent links. "Get link" in a report saves the test state and a snapshot of the report on the server (verdict, reasons, telemetry, thinned-out charts — about 20 KB) and returns a short link /r/<number>. No registration; on a phone the report is shown immediately from the snapshot. The snapshot is sent by the author's browser, so it is not taken on trust: the viewer's page re-runs the test in a background thread and compares the telemetry fingerprint — "result matches" or a recomputed report with a warning. The server validates both the state (like a link from the AI) and the snapshot (schema, sizes). If the server is unavailable, a long link with the test embedded right in the address (#r=…) remains.
  • Clip (the "Clip 12 s" button in a report): the test is recomputed, frames are captured at the required moments of model time and played at exactly 30 per second into MediaRecorder — 960×540, MP4 (or WebM where MP4 is not supported), about 2 MB. With a breakup: 3 s of run-up, 5 s of the slowed-down moment of breakup with a marker, 4 s of the verdict card; without a breakup — the whole test in 8 s plus the card. The clip is downloaded as a file; it is not stored on the server.
  • AI generation limits: per browser (anonymous cookie, no registration) 10 per hour and 40 per day, per address 30 per hour, total daily budget $10. When exceeded — a message saying how long to wait and that examples and editing assumptions are free. Rejected requests never reach the AI. Everything is configured in .env.
  • Cost monitoring — the /admin page (password ADMIN_TOKEN; disabled without it): costs today and in total against the daily budget, generations by day (successful, with an image, time), errors over the week, the last 50 generations, saved reports and their views. The log contains no description text or images, the address is stored only as a salted hash.
  • Two languages — Russian and English. A switch at the top of the panel, ?lang=en, otherwise the browser language. Everything the user sees is translated: the interface, the verdict and the report (phrases as pairs tr('…', '…') in src/core), names of aircraft, parts, assumptions and materials (dictionary src/core/i18n-data.ts). The AI answers in the interface language. A report saved in one language is shown to a viewer in another recomputed in the viewer's language (the telemetry fingerprint does not depend on the language). Still in Russian only: specification validation messages on error, command-line output, /admin.
  • Example gallery — six reference aircraft on the "Input" screen (since stage 4); they do not call the AI.
  • Storage — the SQLite built into Node, a single file (DB_PATH, default var/stand.db). The spec calls for PostgreSQL and object storage: for a single node this is unnecessary, and clips and images are not stored on the server at all. If it grows — move the reports and generations tables to PostgreSQL.
  • Security: CSP headers (own origin only, wasm-unsafe-eval for Rapier), framing forbidden, nosniff; escaping the dist/ folder is blocked; the AI key lives only on the server and only from .env/the environment.
  • Deployment: Dockerfile — a single container, data on the /data volume, port 8080, health check /api/health, TRUST_PROXY=1 (behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS).

Found along the way:

  • Without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY the SDK picked up credentials from the user profile (fixed in stage 5).
  • Node does not go through HTTPS_PROXY on its own — the AI client now goes through the proxy if one is set.

Stage 3: flapping wings, elasticity, inverse problem

npm run stand -- snowbird free                   # ornithopter in free flight
npm run stand -- snowbird tunnel                 # ornithopter in a wind tunnel
npm run stand -- smartbird tunnel --wind 6
npm run stand -- ornithopter tethered --inverse  # what it takes to make it work
  • The tunnel program: the vehicle is fixed in altitude and heading, and a flow at cruise speed blows on it (limits.cruiseSpeed or --wind). The autopilot sweeps wing twist, for each one balances lift against weight with the incidence angle, finds the "thrust = drag" condition and measures three cycles at it (details in the "Physics check" section).
  • Ornithopter references (src/presets/flappers.ts): Festo SmartBird (0.48 kg, 13–23 W) and UTIAS Snowbird (human-powered aircraft of 2010, 600–700 W on the power stroke). The wing has sinusoidal twist, linear along the span.
  • Wing elasticity: first natural bending frequency of the cantilever f₁ = (1.875²/2π)·√(EI/(μL⁴)), for blades — with centrifugal stiffening (Southwell). Loads are passed through a first-mode resonator (3 % damping), and the larger of the elastic and rigid responses is taken. If the drive is faster than f₁, the verdict warns: the rigid-wing model is not applicable.
  • Inverse problem (src/core/inverse.ts, the "Solve inverse problem" button on the stand): a run without failure → how many times stronger and stiffer the material must be at the same density (margins are proportional to strength or modulus), a verification run with that material (up to two refinements), required power (without recovering the wing acceleration energy and with full recovery), which library materials would work, and what material cannot fix (supersonic flow, resonance, lack of lift, thrust < drag).

"Dune" ornithopter (result)

Verdict — "Breaks up": spar wall buckling, margin 0.001. Inverse problem (7–10 s): it needs a material ~2,640 times stronger and stiffer than unidirectional carbon fiber — no such material exists even among theoretical ones: buckling is governed by the elastic modulus, and for graphene and nanotubes it is higher than carbon fiber's only by ~7 times. A check with such a material gives a margin of 1.5, but the vehicle still "Does not fly": it needs ~7,630 MW (2,890 MW with full recovery of wing deceleration energy) against 5 MW. Material cannot fix it: the wingtips reach M 1.8, the 20 Hz drive is 9 times faster than the wing's natural frequency (2.2 Hz).

Stage 2: building from a description

# key — in the .env file (template .env.example) or in an environment variable; it never reaches the browser

How it works (src/server/generate.ts, src/core/design.ts):

  1. Analysis (Claude Opus 5.5, effort low): whether it is an aircraft, its class, parts, what the user specified, what is known about the real machine or from a primary source.
  2. Design (effort medium): the AI fills in a compact "vehicle design" following a strict schema — dimensions, masses, material, power and a list of assumptions. It does not place part coordinates.
  3. The builder lays out parts, joints, actuators and controls — the same way the reference presets are built. Blade coning and initial propeller pitch are computed, not guessed.
  4. Validation of the design and the specification; on violations, the list is returned to the AI for correction, no more than twice.

On the stand, the assumption sliders edit the design and the specification is rebuilt. A fallback model on failure is enabled (fallbacks: "default"). The user's description is data only: the AI does not follow instructions inside it. Limit — 30 generations per hour per address; editing assumptions and running tests are free.

A vehicle is described by a specification (JSON following the schema in src/core/spec.ts); the stand builds a physical model from it, runs it through a test program and issues a verdict according to the rules of the spec.

Layer Model

Power At joint shafts from torque and speed, transmission and tail rotor losses, piston engine power lapse with altitude
