24 materials in five groups (src/core/materials.ts): metals, composites, natural, dry fibers without matrix, laboratory and theoretical (nanotube fiber and bundles, the single-nanotube limit, graphene, metallic glass). Values and references — data/research.md (compiled 2026-11-10, only from open pages). Gaps in the sources are filled by standard rules and listed for each material in estimates; the page shows them next to the material.

Validation against references

Since 2026-11-12, references are validated against real measurements — the table, tolerances and discrepancies are in the "Fifth physics check" section at the beginning of the file (npm run physics -- --validate). The former table in this section compared against the spec's 20–40 % tolerances, and some of its rows were dependent (the Snowbird flapping amplitude was fitted to the pilot's estimate, the frequency — to "16 flaps in 19.3 s", the quadcopter power — averaged over the flight rather than hover).

What was found during validation and how it was fixed

  • Rapier's position motor corrects the angle bypassing velocities — accelerations cannot be computed from it. Actuators are velocity-driven.
  • Rapier's fixed joint is compliant: blades on it lagged behind the hub, and the centrifugal force produced a spurious shaft torque (rotor power was overestimated 17 times). Rigidly connected parts are now a single body.
  • Acceleration from the velocity difference refers to the middle of the step: force moment arms are taken at the same point.
  • Rotor induced inflow was recomputed instantly and oscillated every other step — now with a lag, as in the Pitt–Peters model.
  • Rigid ground contact kills velocity in a single step and produces a spurious acceleration spike. For failure, loads are smoothed to a frequency 5 times above the main drive (no lower than 30 Hz).
  • Uniform induced inflow underestimated R22 power by 21 %. The standard inflow non-uniformity correction κ = 1.15 was introduced (the rotor's inducedFactor parameter).

Tuning you should know about

Full breakdown — the "Review of previous checks for tuning" table in the "Fifth physics check" section.

  • The Cessna spar cross-section is chosen so that the margin at 1 g is about 5.8 (the normal-category ultimate load factor is 5.7) — the wing structure is not in open data.
  • The Ka-26 blade spar wall (9 mm) is chosen to give a margin of about 1.9; the Ka-26 strength verdict is dependent.
  • SmartBird drag is fitted to the L/D ≈ 7 from the Festo paper; the SmartBird thrust margin is therefore not a check.
  • Removed from tuning (2026-11-12): Snowbird flapping amplitude and twist (now from Reichert's thesis), SmartBird drive efficiency (now from the measurement in the paper).
  • R22 blade coning (2°) is chosen so that centrifugal force balances the bending from thrust in hover.
  • Quadcopter blade drag was temporarily raised to 0.03 before the κ correction existed; now it is the original estimate of 0.02.

Crew thresholds

Sustained load factor: severe from 2.5 g, dangerous from 4 g, incapacitation (loss of consciousness without protection) from 6 g — NASA OCHMO-TB-024. Impact: low risk up to 15.2 g (Brinkley model), light-aircraft seat certification limit 26 g. Lethal levels are not given in open primary sources. Vibration (ISO 2631-1): severe from 1.25 m/s², dangerous from 3 m/s²; our vibration is not weighted with the Wk filter.

Flapping-wing power

Two quantities are computed. Without energy recovery: the sum of the positive parts of power over the actuators — the actuator pays for accelerating the wing and for work against the air, while deceleration is free. With full recovery: the signed average over whole cycles — an elastic wing or a spring returns the energy, leaving only the work done on the air. The "Does not fly" verdict is issued if power is insufficient even with recovery; if it is sufficient only with recovery — "at the limit". The no-recovery quantity also includes work against the steady lift on the downstroke: in real ornithopters it is carried by wing elasticity.

Limitations

  • Airplane lateral motion is not modeled: in the flight program the fuselage moves in the vertical plane.
  • Wing downwash at the horizontal stabilizer is not accounted for: the airplane is more stable than the real one.
  • Rotor blades are welded to the hub (the R22 teetering hub is not modeled); root bending is partly relieved by coning.
  • Wheels and skids have no shock absorbers.
  • The wing is a rigid beam with a correction for the first bending mode; higher modes, flutter and bending–aerodynamics coupling are not computed.
  • A flapping wing in forward flight (SmartBird, Snowbird) — with lift and stall lag; the dynamic stall vortex is not accounted for. Flapping in place (the "Dune" ornithopter) — quasi-steady.
  • Strength: spar walls are unidirectional, without ±45° plies; shear buckling, delamination and attachment joints are not computed. Snowbird strength is not checked (see "Strength check").
  • Above M 0.7 sections are flagged "outside the model".

Building a vehicle from a description or an image needs your own server and AI key (npm run api), so it is switched off in the demo; pick one of the examples. The check scripts (npm run check, npm run physics) print outcomes in Russian: ПРОЙДЕН = PASS, РАСХОЖДЕНИЕ = DIVERGENCE (a known, explained mismatch with measurements), ПРОВАЛ = FAIL, СПРАВОЧНО = INFO. The stand UI has a Russian/English switch. R22 in free flight and its stress tests to FAR 27 (2026-11-24) VALIDATE_ONLY=helistress npm run physics -- --validate # the helicopter series vs. the R22 POH and Robinson safety notices (~10 min) VALIDATE_ONLY=heli,r22 npm run physics -- --validate # earlier R22 checks, re-run after the rotor changes npm run check # everything together (both stress sections included): 505 checks — 389 pass, 115 "DIVERGENCE", 1 failure: three new R22 names had no English translation — fixed after the run and checked separately Free flight Until now the helicopter was only ever tested with its body held (hover — vertical only, forward flight — in a "tunnel"). For the stress tests it now flies freely in all six degrees of freedom: Tail rotor as a force (Sim.tailRotorFree, tailRotor.at, tailRotor.channel). The pedals set the tail-rotor blade pitch; thrust comes from BEMT with the flow through the disc (sideslip and yaw rate change it — this is what gives the tail rotor its weathercock effect), and it acts on the boom. Its power is taken from the main rotor shaft, as before. Programmes with the body held keep the old model (thrust = rotor torque / arm). Body rates in the flapping equation. The inertial moment about each hinge is now summed over the blade elements, the same way the loads are: Iβ·β̈ = M + M_g − Σ m·(d × (ω̇ × d + ω × (ω × d)))·ê, with ω the hub's rotation together with the body. When the fuselage pitches, the disc lags behind the shaft and damps it (checked: at q = 0.2 rad/s the disc tilts 0.38° forward relative to the shaft; theory a₁ = −16q/(γΩ) gives about 0.7° for an estimated Lock number of 4.5). Gravity in the flapping equation is now g − a_hub: in a pull-up the blades cone up. No false gyroscope. The blades are rigid Rapier bodies with the flapping laid over them, so when the fuselage turned, Rapier turned the whole spinning rotor with it and sent its gyroscopic moment into the fuselage through the joint — hundreds of N·m per 0.1 rad/s, a false pitch-roll coupling that made free hover diverge. A real hinge cannot transmit it; that moment is now applied to the blade body itself. R22 geometry from the maintenance manual drawing (ch. 16, fig. 16-2, scaled by the 259 in dimension): horizontal stabiliser 34 in span, about 8 in chord, 148 in behind the mast, set 2.8–3.3° nose down; upper and lower fins about 18 and 17 in tall; tail rotor 174 in behind the mast (POH: 172), 73 in above ground. The centre of gravity was 5.4 in behind the mast — outside the R22 envelope (POH fig. on p. 2-5: about 95–102 in, mast at station 100). With the body held it did not matter; in free flight it was a 1000 N·m nose-up moment. The cabin mass is now 0.215 m forward, putting the CG at station 98 (an estimate inside the envelope). The engine as a torque with a power limit. In free flight the mast joint has no Rapier motor (Rapier's velocity motor holds rpm with any torque — the first free runs flew on up to 250 kW with a 97.7 kW engine). A governor holds 104 % rpm with torque up to available power / Ω (minus transmission losses); the tail rotor is driven from the same shaft. When the demand is higher, the rotor rpm droops; in a pull-up it rises above 104 % — the engine cannot brake it. A pilot autopilot (src/core/helipilot.ts): collective holds vertical speed, cyclic holds attitude with rate damping, attitude is set by speed and drift, pedals hold heading or zero sideslip. Free flight against the held "tunnel" trim (which matched Robinson's power data earlier): 60 kt — 42–46 kW vs. 44.8, collective 11.3–11.6° vs. 11.45°; 90 kt — about 77 kW vs. 73.6, collective 12.9–13.9° vs. 13.3°. The series The helicopter takes off, hovers, accelerates, and is moved to 600 m. Criteria where the rules or the POH give one; the rest are measurements. Blade strength in forward flight stays for reference only (see "R22 in forward flight": equivalent spar, hub suspension not published — the root margin is below 1 already in level flight at 90 kt), so blades do not break in this programme and the verdict is not based on it. Test (rule) What is done R22, model Hover out of ground effect 600 m, 1370 lb ✅ 72.4 kW of 97.7; 43 % pedal travel left Cyclic pull-up at 0.6 / 0.9 VNE (§27.337) aft cyclic to +3.5 g, collective fixed 2.2 / 3.2 g — the rotor stalls first (the R22 design limit is not published); rpm rises to 104 % Low-G pushover (prohibited on the R22) forward cyclic to 0.2 g, lateral cyclic and pedals fixed rolls right at 22 °/s — as the POH and SN-11 warn 30 ft/s vertical gust (§27.341) hover / 0.6 VNE / VNE, controls fixed through the gust 1.29 / 1.74 / 1.91 g Full pedal in 0.2 s (§27.351) hover / 0.6 VNE 166 °/s; 81° sideslip at 61 kt (the rule allows up to 90°) Engine failure at 0.9 VNE (§27.143(e)) controls fixed 1 s, then autorotation at 65 kt ✅ 83 % rpm after 1 s, steady 96–104 % (POH: 90–110 %); 1340 ft/min (SN-38: usually below 1500) 1.1 VNE (§27.175, AC 27-1) 112 kt ✅ 40 % forward cyclic left; not enough power for level flight — flown at −4 m/s at full power, rpm 100 %, 7.5 % of blade sections stalled, advancing tip M 0.78. Held level instead, the collective "eats" the rpm (down to 91 %, below the 97 % low-rpm horn) and retreating-blade stall grows to a third of the disc Limitations The engine failure is the last test: the programme ends in autorotation. No vortex ring and no ground contact on the skids, so the vortex ring and dynamic rollover tests are not in the series. The governor is ideal (no lag, no throttle correlator); the engine power does not depend on rpm. A low-rpm test (raising the collective with the throttle fixed) is not in the series. The flapping hinges are at the hub centre. The real R22 has a teetering hinge plus coning hinges slightly off the axis (offset not published). With the hinge at the centre, the blade root 0.45 m out carries the hinge shear × 0.45 m in bending — the hover blade margin is now 3.3 (it was 6.4 with the old flapping equation, which passed a moment "through" the hinge). The R22 load factor limit, transient rpm minimum and teeter stop angle are not published — reported as measured, without a pass/fail. The main-rotor wake on the stabiliser and fins is not modelled. Validation: 5 checks against what a certified R22 does (hover OGE at max weight, autorotation rpm and sink rate, right roll in low G, forward cyclic left at 1.1 VNE) — all pass. Stress tests to FAR 23 — and what they exposed in the physics (2026-11-24) VALIDATE_ONLY=stress npm run physics -- --validate # the stress programme on the Cessna 172S vs. POH and the rules (~7 min) VALIDATE_ONLY=sixdof,cessna npm run physics -- --validate # roll on full aileron, POH tables — re-checked after the aerodynamics changes npm run check # see the R22 section above for the latest full run (505 checks); the run before the helicopter work: 500 checks — 384 pass, 115 "DIVERGENCE", 1 failure ("influence calculation within 60 s": 64.5 s with the CPU busy, 37.8 s alone) The programme New programme "Stress tests (FAR 23)" for fixed-wing aircraft (stress in src/core/programs.ts). Sources for the list and the criteria are in data/stress-tests.md. The aircraft takes off, then flies a series of certification manoeuvres at 1500 m. Each manoeuvre has a target from the rules, a measurement and a pass/fail. The strength criterion everywhere is a safety margin of at least 1.5 at the limit load (§23.303, §23.305). In the browser, setup and recovery between manoeuvres are fast-forwarded; take-off and the manoeuvres themselves play in real time. Test (rule) What is done Cessna 172S, model +3.8 g at VA (§23.333, §23.337) entry at 1.05·VA = 108 kt, pull to the limit, 1 s 3.55 g at 107 kt — the wing stalls first (that is what VA means); margin 1.92 +3.8 g at VC = 33·√(W/S) = 127 kt pull, 1 s 3.79 g, margin 1.84 −1.52 g at VC (§23.337(b)) push, 1 s −1.67 g (the autopilot overshoots by 10 %), margin 3.93 ±50 ft/s gusts at VC (§23.333(c), §23.341) 1 − cos gust over 25 chords, frozen in the air; elevator fixed 3.82 / −1.90 g; the rule's formula gives 3.83 / −1.83; margin 1.80. With a gust applied to the whole aircraft at once it was 3.34 / −1.25 Checked pitch manoeuvre at VA (§23.423) full aft stick to the limit, then forward 3.31 / −0.63 g, margin 2.09 Rolling pull-out (§23.349, §23.455) from a 60° turn at 2/3 of the limit g, full aileron to roll out 82 °/s, margin 2.78 Full rudder at VA (§23.351) step to the peak sideslip, then neutral 13.2°, margin 6.85 Dive to VD = 1.4·VC = 178 kt (§23.251, §23.33) full throttle, rpm held at the red line; 1 s at VD; pull-out 175 kt; windmilling 2940 rpm with the throttle closed (110 % = 2970 allowed); flutter far away Wings-level stall (§23.201) 1 kt/s, power off, controls fixed for 1 s at the break 52 kt (POH: 53 KCAS); bank 5°; 55 m lost (POH: up to 230 ft = 70 m) Turning stall, 30° (§23.203) 1 kt/s 54.5 kt (POH: 57 KCAS); bank −24…+36° (allowed 60/30) Accelerated turning stall (§23.203) 4 kt/s with rising g 62.5 kt; bank −24…+43° One-turn spin (§23.221) full aft stick and rudder at the break not reproduced: the model settles into a spiral (see limitations) What the tests found in the physics The first runs gave margins that jumped by ±30 % from one sample to the next and a roll rate twice the real one. The cause was in the physics, not in the tests: Wing bending had no air damping in free flight. The aerodynamic damping of the first bending mode was computed from the wind-tunnel flow, which is zero when the aircraft flies freely. So the wing rang at 3 % damping after every control input. Now damping follows the current airspeed: about 10–15 % for the Cessna wing in flight (sim.ts, elasticInfo and the load step). In-plane wing bending went through the narrow spar only. When the wing has a torsion box, in-plane bending is now carried by the whole box: spar, upper and lower skins, rear web (section.ts). Stiffness is 17× higher, the spurious 4 Hz in-plane ringing is gone, and the margin in the checked manoeuvre went from 1.41 to over 1.9. One uniform induced angle per wing half → a lifting line. Each strip of the main wings is now a horseshoe vortex. Induced angles come from Biot–Savart over all strips of both halves, solved each step by a Newton step (plain iteration diverges on the saw-tooth mode). Before, lift did not fall off at the tip and antisymmetric loading (ailerons, roll rate) was barely damped by downwash. Flapping wings keep the previous model: their wake is unsteady, and a quasi-steady lifting line made the Snowbird check worse (thrust margin 0.54 → 0.40 against a measured 0.92). The "straight wing in a tunnel" check used a single half-wing and the full-wing formula: the old model silently assumed the missing half. It is now a full rectangular wing of aspect ratio 10, compared with an independent method — Glauert's Fourier-series solution of the lifting line: lift +2.2 %, induced drag within 0.4 %. Control surfaces followed thin-airfoil theory at any deflection. With control.chordFrac (c_f/c) set, two DATCOM corrections are added (sec. 6.1.1.1, digitised in Roskam Part VI): the viscous one (a real surface is weaker than theory) and the nonlinear K'(δ) for large deflections. The method reproduces NACA TR 661 (23012, 0.2c flap) to ±0.03 in Δc_l up to 20°. Set for the Cessna aileron, elevator and rudder. The gust hit the whole aircraft at once. It was a uniform vertical wind, so the tail felt it together with the wing. Now a gust is frozen in the air (sim.gustAt): the aircraft flies through it, and every strip of the wing and the tail sees it at its own position — the tail l_t/V later. That is how the rules' gust alleviation factor is derived. Crew vibration in the stress programme. The vibration measure (ISO 2631, RMS over 2 s) is meant for sustained shaking; gusts and abrupt controls are one-off jolts, already assessed by the g-load by axis and the Brinkley impact model. In this programme vibration is measured only in steady flight between manoeuvres (a note in the report says so). The recovery after each manoeuvre now starts with a smooth 1.5 s unload — the autopilot used to push from 3.7 g to 0.2 g in about a second. Quantity Before After Reference Aileron power C_lδa, 1/rad 0.48 0.30 JSBSim 0.23, UIUC 0.18 (calculations) Roll damping C_lp −0.62 −0.48 JSBSim −0.47 pb/2V on full aileron, 104 kt 0.24 0.18 Cessna 177B in flight 0.09 (NASA CR-2337) — divergence Cruise power vs. POH table, mean −6.6 % −2.8 % POH fig. 5-8 Rate of climb, 0 / 8000 ft +15 / +16 % +10 / +5 % POH fig. 5-7 Stall, flaps up −0.4 % +0.4 % POH 53 KCAS POH section of the checks (24) 16 pass, 8 divergences 14 pass, 10 divergences climb at 8000 ft now passes; top speed at 8000 ft (−4.3 %, limited by the 2700 rpm of the "light" propeller) and three cruise rpm rows went just over tolerance Why it diverges Roll rate: still twice the Cessna 177B in flight. That is a different aircraft (cantilever wing, its own ailerons). In the test the pedals were held, so adverse yaw built 8–11° of sideslip, which slows the roll through dihedral effect. The model has no aileron hinge gaps and almost no adverse yaw. The calculated C172 models give 0.12–0.15. Propeller rpm in cruise is 2–4 % high (the known "light propeller", see the propeller section). With the lower drag of the lifting line it shows up in more rows: 3 of the cruise rpm checks went just over their 2 % tolerance. The 30° turning stall is 4.4 % below the POH: the programme detects the stall by the share of stalled strips (30 %), the certification test by the nose drop or the stick reaching its stop. Limitations The spin is not reproduced. With full aft stick and rudder the model sits at α ≈ 14° in a spiral. Autorotation needs rotary-balance data for the wing beyond the stall, which strip theory does not have. The step is reported as "not tested". Strength margins belong to the equivalent cantilever spar (its wall is an estimate; the strut is not in the strength calculation). They are not a check of the real airframe. The autopilot is a test pilot with limits: at VA the wing stalls at 3.55 g before reaching 3.8 g, and −1.52 g overshoots to −1.67 g. Both are shown as measured. The helicopter series is described in the next section up (R22 in free flight). Human: power vs. duration, g-loads by axis and time (2026-11-23) VALIDATE_ONLY=human npm run physics -- --validate # checks for this section (seconds) npm run check # everything together: 493 checks — 382 pass, 111 "DIVERGENCE", no failures The full run had one failure: a verdict text contained a number that was not in the telemetry. It was fixed after the run and checked separately. The new crew model did not change the verdicts of earlier tests. What was added to the core Human as an engine (powerplant.engine: { type: 'human', level: 'healthy' | 'champion', durationS }). Available power is what a person can sustain for a given time. Source: NASA SP-3006 (1973) curves, fig. 18-15: healthy men and champions. Endurance in the report comes from the inverse curve: how long the person can last at the required power. Crew g-loads by body axis and duration (src/core/crew.ts, CrewLoad). Previously there was a g-load module checked against a single threshold; now: Sustained. Averages along ±Gx, Gy, ±Gz over windows from 1 to 1200 s are compared against two curves: the NASA-STD-3001 limit (rev. C, 2022) for a healthy crew — "severe"; average tolerance of healthy people (Chambers 1963, via SP-3006) — "dangerous". Loss of consciousness (G-LOC). +Gz averaged over 5 s from 5.4 g (Cochran 1954, unprotected) — "no one left to fly the aircraft". Impact. Brinkley model: spinal response along three axes, coefficients from NASA/TM-2013-217380. The combined axis index β is compared with NASA limits for low (< 0.5 %) and moderate (0.5–5 %) injury risk. The old "sustained / peak g-load" values remain in the telemetry for comparison. The crew verdict names whatever exceeded its limit: axis, window, limit, impact, vibration. What the checks showed Check Result Healthy human power (SP-3006) vs. Whitt & Wilson 1982, 5 points pass, 0–4 % Champion power vs. professional cyclists (Pinot & Grappe 2014, Valenzuela 2022, Gallo 2022, Wilkie 1960), 14 points 10 pass; 4 divergences at efforts of 30 s – 5 min: modern racers are 11–18 % higher Daedalus: 3.1 W/kg for 6 hours info: extending the curve gives 227 W (beyond the data) +Gz tolerance vs. test pilots (Chambers & Hitchcock 1963): 9 g — 8 s, 8 g — 29 s, 6 g — 157 s 2 pass (3 and 2 %), 1 divergence +16 % at 8 s Brinkley model vs. rocket sled tests (Stapp; SP-3006), 7 tests all tests with injury are above the low-risk limit: pass Info. The Brinkley model also places impacts survived without harm in the moderate-risk band: −Gx 45 g for 0.09 s and +Gx 30 g for 0.11 s. NASA limits are for design, with margin. The pulse shapes in the tests were not recorded: a trapezoid is assumed. Loss of consciousness across different centrifuges: Cochran 5.4 ± 0.9 g, Zarriello 5.3 ± 0.8, Kasture 4.89 ± 0.67, Chiang 5.1 ± 0.9. The others use different endpoints: loss of peripheral or central vision, which comes earlier. Limitations Human power does not depend on altitude. Above 1500 m aerobic power drops; in the model it does not. Body mass is not given in the SP-3006 curves: power is absolute, in watts. The NASA limit assumes a restraint harness and an anti-g suit. Chambers tolerance is voluntary, for healthy subjects. There is no tolerance curve for Gy; the NASA emergency limit is used instead. Consciousness under negative g (−Gz) is not assessed separately — only via the curves. The occupant sits facing forward; body axes coincide with the airframe axes. Structure: wing flutter and divergence, laminated composites (2026-11-23) VALIDATE_ONLY=structure npm run physics -- --validate # checks for this section (seconds) npm run check # everything together: 470 checks — 364 pass, 106 "DIVERGENCE" (full run 2026-11-23 — 469 checks; the strut-braced Cessna flutter check was added after it and passed separately; the "influence calculation within 60 s" check did not fit in that run — 130 s with the CPU busy with other programs) What was added to the core Wing flutter and divergence (src/core/aeroelastic.ts). A beam with an elastic axis; mode shapes by the finite element method (bending — Euler–Bernoulli beam, torsion — a rod, coupling — via the offset of the center of mass); the four lowest are used. Supports: the root is clamped or hinged; the strut (structure.strut) is a vertical support at its attachment point on the chord: it couples deflection with twist. Theodorsen unsteady aerodynamics, strip by strip. Solved by the p-k method: at each speed the roots of the characteristic polynomial are found. Flutter is the speed where an oscillation stops decaying. Divergence is where torsion loses static stability. Flutter in the stand (Sim.flutterInfo). Computed for a stationary wing with a specified torsion box structure.torsionBox — the skin between the spars that carries torsion. From the part's structure the following are taken: EI — of the spar; GJ — of the torsion box, by the Bredt formula; elastic axis — the middle of the torsion box; mass distribution — the spar at sparAt, the skin along the chord. Without a torsion box the torsional stiffness is unknown, and flutter is not checked. Cessna 172S: torsion box and strut are estimates (assumptions "Wing torsion box skin" and "Strut attachment"). There is no data: the Cessna structural repair manual (SESR04) gives only materials; there are no wing stiffnesses or frequency measurements. Spars at 20 and 65 % chord, skin 0.020 in, strut to the front spar at 2.6 m from the centerline, root hinged. Result: no wing flutter up to 270 m/s, divergence from 690 m/s for any combination of estimates (skin 0.016–0.025 in, spars ±5 % chord, strut ±0.3 m). This is a plausibility check: the aircraft is certified, and the regulations require freedom from flutter up to 1.2·V_D ≈ 112 m/s. Without the strut the same cantilever diverges at 192 m/s, and the first frequency drops from 12.8 to 6.5 Hz. Aileron flutter (on the real aircraft they are mass-balanced) is not computed. Flutter in the verdict. If the test speed reached the flutter or divergence speed — "Breaks up". If the margin is below 20 %, a warning (CS-23.629 requires 1.2 times the design dive speed). The report has a line "Wing flutter and divergence". Laminated composite (src/core/laminate.ts, structure.layup: fractions of 0°, ±45°, 90° plies). Stiffness — by classical laminate theory. Strength — by maximum strain in ply axes, with cracked plies switched off: fibers break — the laminate has failed; the matrix cracks — the ply loses transverse stiffness and the load is redistributed. Without a layup, the composite is unidirectional along the span, as before. Materials now have Yt and Yc — ply strength transverse to the fibers. What the checks showed Check Model Measured Result Goland wing (computational benchmark) 137.0 m/s, 68 rad/s 137 m/s, ≈70 rad/s pass NACA TN 1594, run 96 (air) 104.3 m/s 101.7 m/s pass, +2.6 % run 60 (air) 100.0 m/s 103.0 m/s pass, −2.9 % run 5 (Freon-12, ρ four times higher) 57.3 m/s 55.4 m/s pass, +3.4 % Flutter frequency 24.6 / 24.8 / 27.2 Hz 22.1 / 22.0 / 25.2 Hz divergence +8–13 % Frequencies: bending, second bending, torsion 6.65 / 41.6 / 48.6 Hz 6.25–6.45 / 35.8–39.2 / 44.6–47.6 Hz divergence +5–10 % Cessna 172S, torsion box and strut are estimates no flutter up to 270 m/s, divergence ≥ 690 m/s regulations: none up to 1.2·V_D ≈ 112 m/s pass (plausibility) NCAMP laminates, compressive modulus (3 layups) pass, 0.1–0.8 % NCAMP laminates, tensile modulus (4 layups) 1 pass, 3 divergences +5–6 % Tensile strength: 10/80/10 / 25/50/25 / 50/40/10 / [0/90] 463 / 879 / 1410 / 1287 MPa 462.5 / 717 / 1215 / 1166 MPa 1 pass, 3 divergences +10…+23 % Compressive strength: 10/80/10 / 25/50/25 / 50/40/10 422 / 661 / 1016 MPa 465 / 600 / 835 MPa 1 pass, 2 divergences +10 and +22 % Why it diverges Flutter frequency. 8–13 % higher than the real one, even with four modes: the cause is strip theory (no tip losses), not the number of modes. NACA's 1949 calculation with the same theory gave the same error: 25.27 Hz vs. 22.1. The flutter speed still agrees. Natural frequencies. The clamp in the model is perfectly rigid; the real one in the tunnel is more compliant. Laminate strength is overestimated. A calculation based on the failure strain of a unidirectional ply (1.58 %) does not know that fibers in a laminate break earlier: a quasi-isotropic one fails at 1.25 %. This is a known effect: stress concentration at specimen edges, cracking of neighboring plies, interlaminar stresses at free edges. So the model rates parts with a layup as stronger than real ones — by up to 20 %. No correction factor was fitted. Ply compression. NCAMP back-calculated the ply compressive strength from a cross-ply specimen using this same theory, so compression is not a fully independent check. Limitations Strip theory: no tip losses, no compressibility. Above M ≈ 0.5 the flutter speed is overestimated. The strut is accounted for only in flutter: spar strength is still computed as for an equivalent cantilever. Flutter of propeller blades and flapping wings is not computed: the oscillations there are of a different nature. Wing-mounted masses (tanks, engines) are not included in flutter. Nonlinear large-deflection flutter (as on the Pazy wing) is outside the model. They were added after the run; the translation check passes separately. What was added to the core Blades on flapping hinges (flapping on the rotor). This is how the R22 hub is built per the POH: teetering, with coning hinges. Each blade's flapping has its own equation: Iβ·β̈ = M_aero + M_grav − Iβ·Ω²·(β₀ + β). Centrifugal force restores the blade at exactly once per revolution. The blade stays a rigid body in Rapier. Flapping is superimposed on the position and velocity of the sections in the aerodynamics and loads, and the moment about the hinge is removed from the body — it is not transmitted to the hub. Coning settles by itself: 1.8° in hover (the previous constant-coning estimate was 2°). Blade loads include the blade's acceleration due to flapping (angular, centripetal, Coriolis). Cyclic pitch (cyclic): blade angle += cos·cos ψ + sin·sin ψ by azimuth. The rotor axis for the flow is the normal to the tip-path plane. Freewheel clutch (freewheel): the engine disengages; rpm is set by the flow and the rotor inertia. The tail rotor is driven by the main rotor and brakes it with its profile power. The joint motor in Rapier cannot be switched off: with zero coefficients the joint becomes rigid. So the shaft joint is recreated without a motor. Main rotor power is computed with sign. Coriolis forces rock the shaft twice per revolution, averaging zero. Taking only the positive part overestimates power fourfold. Tail rotor thrust is based on torque smoothed over 0.5 s. Forward flight in a "tunnel" (src/cli/rotorflight.ts): the fuselage is free vertically, with flow from the front. Autopilot: collective holds vertical speed, and in autorotation — rpm; longitudinal cyclic balances drag; lateral cyclic balances tail rotor thrust. The cause was known: the propeller in the model is a momentum disk with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller has no set rpm. The rpm settles where engine torque equals the torque the propeller absorbs. At low speed the propeller is "heavier", rpm is below 2700, and the engine delivers less power. The rule is the same: the references are only independent 172S POH data (data/research.md, part 4.2), nothing was tuned to fit them. What was done in the core src/core/propeller.ts (new) — a blade element propeller model with momentum theory on each annulus: axial and tangential induced velocities, Prandtl tip and root losses. At each radius a single equation is solved for the inflow angle φ (the Ning 2014 formulation, written for a propeller): Ωr·(sin²φ − σ'·Cn/4F) − V·(sin φ·cos φ + σ'·Ct/4F) = 0. There is no singularity at V = 0; the root is found by bisection. Section coefficients come from the shared airfoilCoeffs model (full range of angles, Prandtl–Glauert, compressibility drag rise from the sixth review). There is propellerEquilibrium — the equilibrium rpm for a given engine torque. src/core/sim.ts — the propeller drive has an optional fixedPitch block. If it is set, rpm is a state variable: I·dΩ/dt = Q_engine − Q_prop. Engine torque = throttle × power/ω_rated × altitude lapse. Without the block everything is as before (a disk with an efficiency — like a constant-speed propeller; projects from design.ts are built this way). At zero throttle the propeller windmills and brakes the aircraft. Sample has propRpm, propEfficiency. IO-360-L2A engine. At full throttle torque is constant and power is proportional to rpm. The basis is type certificate EASA.IM.E.032 (Issue 03, 2022, sec. 6 "Ratings", full throttle at sea level): 119 kW (160 hp) at 2400 rpm and 134 kW (180 hp) at 2700 rpm. That is 474 N·m at both points, to within 0.1 % (data/research.md, 4.2, item 7). Below 2400 rpm there are no data points; constant torque there is an assumption. New field powerplant.ratedRpm = 2700. Flight program (programs.ts). At full throttle in level flight at sea level the fixed-pitch propeller would spin the engine up to 3080 rpm. So the program, like a pilot, pulls back the throttle and holds no more than ratedRpm: the 2700 redline (POH, section 2). The vorticity C_V is the difference between the attached-flow normal force and the force with lagged separation (in the scheme C_N^C·(1 − K_N)); its increments feed into the vortex normal force with lag Tv while the vortex is over the airfoil (τ_v ≤ Tvl from stall onset by the criterion). Then the vortex force decays with Tv/2; if stall continues, after Tvl + Tsh the next vortex begins (Tsh = 2(1 − w)/St). Stall onset is the lagged angle beyond the static stall angle, i.e. C_N1 is the static stall normal force. The constants are the published ones for NACA 0012, not tuned to the references: Tp 1.7, Tf 3.0, Tv 6.0 (Leishman & Beddoes; the same numbers are the OpenFAST AeroDyn defaults), Tvl 7.0 (Leishman & Beddoes 1986 for NACA 0012 at M 0.3; the OpenFAST default is 11), St 0.19. Not introduced: the Tf and Tv corrections by cycle stage (multipliers 0.25…4 in OpenFAST), the vortex suction force and pitching moment. It acts only on parts with unsteady flow — that is, flapping wings; propellers, airplanes and helicopters are not affected. Also checked with Tvl = 11 (OpenFAST): the peak C_L is the same, only the post-peak decay changes. M_dd (where dc_d/dM = 0.1) at α = 0, 4, 6, 8° fell on the line 0.800 − 0.31·c_l with a scatter of ±0.02, i.e. κ_A = 0.92, s = 0.31. Korn's classic s = 0.1 is for airfoils at their design c_l; for a loaded NACA 0012 M_dd drops three times faster (with that s, Korn–Lock at α = 4–8° gave almost no rise where c_d had already doubled in the experiment). The −t/c term is confirmed by the text of the same report: a blade with an NACA 0015 tip diverges at a c̄_l 0.10 lower than NACA 0012, and 0.03 of thickness = 0.31 × 0.10. 6-series airfoils behave differently: their nose suction peak is smaller, and M_dd depends weakly on c_l. There κ_int is the ratio of the induced power of the pair to two isolated rotors at the same disk loading, i.e. the same definition as in the model. The model describes steady flight within 4–9 % in power, and stall accurately. Climb is strongly overestimated (+50–60 %): in the model the propeller is a disc with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller at low speed turns below 2700 rpm, with an efficiency of about 0.6. The "Does not fly" verdicts for an overloaded aircraft are therefore optimistic: the model may pass an aircraft that in reality will not climb. Rotors in hover. The model with κ = 1.15 correctly describes a twisted rotor (Carpenter, within 5 %) and the Harrington single rotor. For an untwisted rotor and at low Reynolds numbers (TN 626) it underestimates power by 4–11 %. For the real R22 the discrepancy is 12 %. Ornithopter free flight (2026-11-11) The Snowbird numbers in this and the following sections predate the fifth physics check. With the kinematics from Reichert's thesis (0.65 Hz, tip stroke ±1.0 m, twist ±7°) the Snowbird model does not stay in the air — see "Fifth physics check". npm run stand -- smartbird free # trim search in the stream, then free flight npm run report -- snowbird free The new free program is "Ornithopter free flight" (src/core/programs.ts). On the page it is the default for SmartBird and Snowbird. Trim search — the same wind-tunnel autopilot: the body is fixed in the oncoming flow, and the wing incidence and twist are tuned. On the page this part runs accelerated (1–5 s). Release. The oncoming flow is converted into the vehicle's velocity: velocity V is added to every body, and to the wind as well (Sim.boost). The flow around the vehicle does not change. The body is released: forward and vertical motion are free, heading and body pitch are held. Flight — 16 flaps, but no less than 8 s. Once per flap the autopilot corrects the wing incidence (altitude) and the twist (speed). How the autopilot works. A wing damps its own sink: as it descends, it meets the flow at a higher angle. So over a flap what settles is not an acceleration but a sink rate proportional to the deviation of the incidence from the trim value: v_y = V·Δθ. On each flap the autopilot refines the trim incidence and adds a correction that removes 35% of the altitude error per flap. Speed is handled the same way, through twist. The first version of the autopilot assumed the angle sets acceleration and held neither altitude nor speed: SmartBird lost 0.43 m and 5% of its speed in 8 s. The measure of flight is total energy (altitude + V²/2g): its loss over the distance flown equals the thrust deficit. A loss above 20% of drag is "Does not fly", 5 to 20% is "Flies at the limit". Power is compared with the available power the same way as in the wind tunnel. Strength check (2026-11-11) npm run physics -- --strength # strength checks only, a few seconds The strength calculation (src/core/strength.ts, src/core/section.ts, loads — src/core/sim.ts) was verified against strength-of-materials formulas on individual sections and on a wing in a flow: 25 checks, all pass. What was verified Discrepancy Box area and moment of inertia, bending stress, torsion (Bredt), shear, equivalent stress (von Mises), margin to rounding Critical wall stress: compression, flapwise bending, in-plane (chordwise) bending to rounding Tube: bending in two planes to rounding Fatigue: Basquin curve, Goodman correction up to 0.1% Wing in steady flow: root stresses from lift and drag 0.5% Elastic wing near resonance (drive at half the natural frequency): stress range × 1.33 0.2% Four bugs were found and fixed: Composite walls buckled "like metal". The critical stress was computed with the formula for an isotropic plate using the longitudinal modulus. In a composite the wall is also held by the transverse modulus, which is several times lower. Now the plate stiffness is B = √(Q₁₁·Q₂₂) + Q₁₂ + 2·Q₆₆, σ_cr = k/4 · π²t²/(6w²) · B. For unidirectional carbon fibre (135 / 10 / 5 GPa) B = 50 GPa instead of 297 GPa — 5.9 times less. For metal the formula reduces to the previous one. The transverse modulus and shear modulus were added to the library for the carbon fibres, glass fibre, aramid and spruce; where no data exist, they are taken from a generic carbon fibre and marked as estimates. One critical stress for the whole section. The lower of two was taken (flange in compression, web in flapwise bending) and compared with the highest compression at any corner. Now each of the four box walls is checked separately: its own width, its own stress distribution, coefficient k from 4 (uniform compression) to 23.9 (bending in the plane of the wall) per EN 1993-1-5, Table 4.1. For the tube, bending in two planes was added arithmetically — the stress was overestimated by up to √2 times. Now it uses the resultant moment. Fatigue was computed only for the upper flange, without in-plane bending. Now it uses the worst of the four corners of the section. Unsteady flow over a flapping wing (2026-11-11) npm run physics -- --unsteady # unsteady-model checks only, a few seconds For a surface with aero.unsteady: true (SmartBird and Snowbird) lift is computed with flow memory (src/core/aero.ts, src/core/sim.ts): Lift lag — the Wagner function in Jones's approximation, φ(s) = 1 − 0.165·e^(−0.0455·s) − 0.335·e^(−0.3·s), s — distance in semichords. The angle of attack is taken from the downwash at the ¾-chord point (including the section's pitch rate). The force is perpendicular to the effective flow: when it lags, it is tilted backwards and the stroke thrust is lower. Stall lag — a simplified Beddoes–Leishman model (trailing-edge separation): two first-order lags, Tp = 1.7 and Tf = 3.0 semichords. The constants are taken from the literature for the NACA 0012 airfoil and were not tuned. With a rapid increase in angle, lift exceeds the static maximum. Added mass — both from flapping and from the section's rotation in the flow. Physics verification (2026-11-11) npm run physics # only the checks against general laws, about 2 minutes npm run check # everything together (236 checks as of 2026-11-12), all pass The core was re-read from scratch and checked against laws that do not depend on the program (src/cli/physics.ts): Check Computed Formula Discrepancy Free fall, distance in 2 s 19.63 m g·t²/2 0.03 % Terminal fall velocity 17.90 m/s √(2mg / ρ·C_D·S) 0.01 % Load factor in the seat: falling / on the ground 0.000 g / 1.000 g 0 / 1 — Pendulum, 90° swing: period 2.360 s 4·K(sin 45°)·√(2L/3g) 0.3 % Pendulum: energy loss over three periods 1.96 % 0 numerical damping, ~0.7 % per period Centrifugal force at the blade root 14.21 kN ω²·Σm·r 0.00 % Thrust of a flapping wing in a flow 1.634 N ¼·ρ·c·a·θ₀²·ω²·R³/3 (Garrick at F = 1) 1.9 % Flapping energy balance: shaft power 32.65 W thrust × flow velocity 0.07 % Wing without drag at an angle thrust 0 d'Alembert's paradox exact Symmetry: ornithopter side force 1·10⁻¹⁰ N out of 1.7·10⁷ N 0 — Half the time step: ornithopter, R22, Cessna — same result 0.01–1.7 % What was found and fixed: The wind-tunnel autopilot got stuck. Thrust depends non-monotonically on wing twist: too little and the wing stalls, too much and it "feathers" and produces no thrust. The old controller turned the twist "in one direction only", considered balance reached with a thrust shortfall of up to 1 % of weight (while the verdict required strictly ≥ 0), and did not allow the incidence angle above the stall angle. Because of this SmartBird "did not hold its weight" and Snowbird "did not pull". Now the twist is swept over the whole range, lift is balanced by the secant method, the T = D regime is searched for on the unstalled branch, and strength and peaks are computed only at the regime found (parts do not break during the search trials). Flapping power was overstated by a factor of two. It was computed as a sum of absolute values: braking the wing cost as much as accelerating it. An actuator that brakes a part spends no energy. Now there are two quantities: without recovery of braking energy (sum of the positive parts over the actuators) and with full recovery (signed average over whole cycles — the work done on the air). For the "Dune" ornithopter these are 7,630 and 2,890 MW instead of 12,400 MW. The label "with full recovery" was previously attached to a number that was not that. Averages over an incomplete cycle. Power and lift were averaged over windows of 1 s and 0.5 s — for slow flapping (Snowbird, 0.83 Hz) that is not a whole cycle. Now the windows are multiples of the cycle. Snowbird data were guesses even though they are published (data/research.md): wing area 29.2 m² (was 39 m² "so that it holds its weight"), flight mass 114.3 kg, 16 flaps in 19.3 s = 0.83 Hz (was 0.6), pilot power 600–700 W on the power stroke (was 300 W). With the real area the aircraft flies at C_L = 1.24 — right at the stall. SmartBird drag was tuned to the published lift-to-drag ratio L/D ≈ 7 (was ~10). What came out after the fixes: These are results of the quasi-steady model; after accounting for unsteadiness the numbers are different — see the section above. SmartBird — "Flies": thrust margin 2–6 % of weight, 10.7 W for flapping without energy recovery (6.8 W with recovery) versus 13 W per the paper (level flight at 4.7 m/s without servos; 18 W with them): −17 %. Snowbird — "Flies at the limit", as the spec requires: thrust is short by 3.8 N (9 % of drag, 0.34 % of weight), power suffices only with energy recovery (309 W; without recovery 700 W against 650 W). In the record of the real flight total energy and speed were also slowly decreasing. Caveat: the flapping amplitude is not published and was chosen (±3°) so that the work per flap matches the pilot's estimate; the power check is therefore not independent. New verdict rules for flapping flight: A thrust shortfall of less than 20 % of drag (the spec's tolerance for reference aircraft) is "at the limit", not "does not fly": the model does not know drag more precisely than that. If power suffices only with recovery of the wings' braking energy — "at the limit" with an explanation; if it is insufficient even with recovery — "does not fly". Unsteadiness warning: at a reduced frequency k ≥ 0.1 the steady-flow model overstates flapping thrust — by Theodorsen–Garrick theory for an airfoil, by a factor of 2.1–2.2 at k ≈ 0.3. For SmartBird and Snowbird unsteadiness is now taken into account (section above); the warning remains for surfaces without unsteady. Known numerical errors (not fixed, covered by checks): The velocity-driven actuator falls short of the amplitude by about 1 % at 120 steps per cycle and by about 3 % in power at 40 steps per cycle (ornithopter); it goes away as the time step decreases. The engine computes in single precision: the centre of mass of an ornithopter in vacuum drifts by 5.6 mm in 3.5 s with a fuselage travel of ±515 mm (1 %); the error grows as the time step decreases — this is rounding, not integration. Stage 3: flapping wings, elasticity, inverse problem npm run stand -- snowbird free # ornithopter in free flight npm run stand -- snowbird tunnel # ornithopter in a wind tunnel npm run stand -- smartbird tunnel --wind 6 npm run stand -- ornithopter tethered --inverse # what it takes to make it work The tunnel program: the vehicle is fixed in altitude and heading, and a flow at cruise speed blows on it (limits.cruiseSpeed or --wind). The autopilot sweeps wing twist, for each one balances lift against weight with the incidence angle, finds the "thrust = drag" condition and measures three cycles at it (details in the "Physics check" section). Ornithopter references (src/presets/flappers.ts): Festo SmartBird (0.48 kg, 13–23 W) and UTIAS Snowbird (human-powered aircraft of 2010, 600–700 W on the power stroke). The wing has sinusoidal twist, linear along the span. Wing elasticity: first natural bending frequency of the cantilever f₁ = (1.875²/2π)·√(EI/(μL⁴)), for blades — with centrifugal stiffening (Southwell). Loads are passed through a first-mode resonator (3 % damping), and the larger of the elastic and rigid responses is taken. If the drive is faster than f₁, the verdict warns: the rigid-wing model is not applicable. Inverse problem (src/core/inverse.ts, the "Solve inverse problem" button on the stand): a run without failure → how many times stronger and stiffer the material must be at the same density (margins are proportional to strength or modulus), a verification run with that material (up to two refinements), required power (without recovering the wing acceleration energy and with full recovery), which library materials would work, and what material cannot fix (supersonic flow, resonance, lack of lift, thrust < drag). "Dune" ornithopter (result) Verdict — "Breaks up": spar wall buckling, margin 0.001. Inverse problem (7–10 s): it needs a material ~2,640 times stronger and stiffer than unidirectional carbon fiber — no such material exists even among theoretical ones: buckling is governed by the elastic modulus, and for graphene and nanotubes it is higher than carbon fiber's only by ~7 times. A check with such a material gives a margin of 1.5, but the vehicle still "Does not fly": it needs ~7,630 MW (2,890 MW with full recovery of wing deceleration energy) against 5 MW. Material cannot fix it: the wingtips reach M 1.8, the 20 Hz drive is 9 times faster than the wing's natural frequency (2.2 Hz). What was found during validation and how it was fixed Rapier's position motor corrects the angle bypassing velocities — accelerations cannot be computed from it. Actuators are velocity-driven. Rapier's fixed joint is compliant: blades on it lagged behind the hub, and the centrifugal force produced a spurious shaft torque (rotor power was overestimated 17 times). Rigidly connected parts are now a single body. Acceleration from the velocity difference refers to the middle of the step: force moment arms are taken at the same point. Rotor induced inflow was recomputed instantly and oscillated every other step — now with a lag, as in the Pitt–Peters model. Rigid ground contact kills velocity in a single step and produces a spurious acceleration spike. For failure, loads are smoothed to a frequency 5 times above the main drive (no lower than 30 Hz). Uniform induced inflow underestimated R22 power by 21 %. The standard inflow non-uniformity correction κ = 1.15 was introduced (the rotor's inducedFactor parameter). Tuning you should know about Full breakdown — the "Review of previous checks for tuning" table in the "Fifth physics check" section. The Cessna spar cross-section is chosen so that the margin at 1 g is about 5.8 (the normal-category ultimate load factor is 5.7) — the wing structure is not in open data. The Ka-26 blade spar wall (9 mm) is chosen to give a margin of about 1.9; the Ka-26 strength verdict is dependent. SmartBird drag is fitted to the L/D ≈ 7 from the Festo paper; the SmartBird thrust margin is therefore not a check. Removed from tuning (2026-11-12): Snowbird flapping amplitude and twist (now from Reichert's thesis), SmartBird drive efficiency (now from the measurement in the paper). R22 blade coning (2°) is chosen so that centrifugal force balances the bending from thrust in hover. Quadcopter blade drag was temporarily raised to 0.03 before the κ correction existed; now it is the original estimate of 0.02. Crew thresholds Sustained load factor: severe from 2.5 g, dangerous from 4 g, incapacitation (loss of consciousness without protection) from 6 g — NASA OCHMO-TB-024. Impact: low risk up to 15.2 g (Brinkley model), light-aircraft seat certification limit 26 g. Lethal levels are not given in open primary sources. Vibration (ISO 2631-1): severe from 1.25 m/s², dangerous from 3 m/s²; our vibration is not weighted with the Wk filter. Flapping-wing power Two quantities are computed. Without energy recovery: the sum of the positive parts of power over the actuators — the actuator pays for accelerating the wing and for work against the air, while deceleration is free. With full recovery: the signed average over whole cycles — an elastic wing or a spring returns the energy, leaving only the work done on the air. The "Does not fly" verdict is issued if power is insufficient even with recovery; if it is sufficient only with recovery — "at the limit". The no-recovery quantity also includes work against the steady lift on the downstroke: in real ornithopters it is carried by wing elasticity. Limitations Airplane lateral motion is not modeled: in the flight program the fuselage moves in the vertical plane. Wing downwash at the horizontal stabilizer is not accounted for: the airplane is more stable than the real one. Rotor blades are welded to the hub (the R22 teetering hub is not modeled); root bending is partly relieved by coning. Wheels and skids have no shock absorbers. The wing is a rigid beam with a correction for the first bending mode; higher modes, flutter and bending–aerodynamics coupling are not computed. A flapping wing in forward flight (SmartBird, Snowbird) — with lift and stall lag; the dynamic stall vortex is not accounted for. Flapping in place (the "Dune" ornithopter) — quasi-steady. Strength: spar walls are unidirectional, without ±45° plies; shear buckling, delamination and attachment joints are not computed. Snowbird strength is not checked (see "Strength check"). Above M 0.7 sections are flagged "outside the model".

blocks.html_en: • Tail rotor as a force (Sim.tailRotorFree, tailRotor.at, tailRotor.channel). The pedals set the tail-rotor blade pitch; thrust comes from BEMT with the flow through the disc (sideslip and yaw rate change it — this is what gives the tail rotor its weathercock effect), and it acts on the boom. The inertial moment about each hinge is now summed over the blade elements, the same way the loads are: Iβ·β̈ = M + M_g − Σ m·(d × (ω̇ × d + ω × (ω × d)))·ê, with ω the hub's rotation together with the body. When the fuselage pitches, the disc lags behind the shaft and damps it (checked: at q = 0.2 rad/s the disc tilts 0.38° forward relative to the shaft; theory a₁ = −16q/(γΩ) gives about 0.7° for an estimated Lock number of 4.5). Gravity in the flapping equation is now g − a_hub: in a pull-up the blades cone up.

blocks.html_en: • No false gyroscope. The blades are rigid Rapier bodies with the flapping laid over them, so when the fuselage turned, Rapier turned the whole spinning rotor with it and sent its gyroscopic moment into the fuselage through the joint — hundreds of N·m per 0.1 rad/s, a false pitch-roll coupling that made free hover diverge. A real hinge cannot transmit it; that moment is now applied to the blade body itself.

blocks.html_en: • Wing bending had no air damping in free flight. The aerodynamic damping of the first bending mode was computed from the wind-tunnel flow, which is zero when the aircraft flies freely. So the wing rang at 3 % damping after every control input. Now damping follows the current airspeed: about 10–15 % for the Cessna wing in flight (sim.ts, elasticInfo and the load step).

sentences.en: Wing bending had no air damping in free flight.
The aerodynamic damping of the first bending mode was computed from the wind-tunnel flow, which is zero when the aircraft flies freely.
So the wing rang at 3 % damping after every control input.
Now damping follows the current airspeed: about 10–15 % for the Cessna wing in flight (sim.ts, elasticInfo and the load step).

blocks.html_en: • In-plane wing bending went through the narrow spar only. When the wing has a torsion box, in-plane bending is now carried by the whole box: spar, upper and lower skins, rear web (section.ts). Stiffness is 17× higher, the spurious 4 Hz in-plane ringing is gone, and the margin in the checked manoeuvre went from 1.41 to over 1.9.

sentences.en: In-plane wing bending went through the narrow spar only.
When the wing has a torsion box, in-plane bending is now carried by the whole box: spar, upper and lower skins, rear web (section.ts).
Stiffness is 17× higher, the spurious 4 Hz in-plane ringing is gone, and the margin in the checked manoeuvre went from 1.41 to over 1.9.

blocks.html_en: • One uniform induced angle per wing half → a lifting line. Each strip of the main wings is now a horseshoe vortex. Induced angles come from Biot–Savart over all strips of both halves, solved each step by a Newton step (plain iteration diverges on the saw-tooth mode). Before, lift did not fall off at the tip and antisymmetric loading (ailerons, roll rate) was barely damped by downwash. Flapping wings keep the previous model: their wake is unsteady, and a quasi-steady lifting line made the Snowbird check worse (thrust margin 0.54 → 0.40 against a measured 0.92). The "straight wing in a tunnel" check used a single half-wing and the full-wing formula: the old model silently assumed the missing half. It is now a full rectangular wing of aspect ratio 10, compared with an independent method — Glauert's Fourier-series solution of the lifting line: lift +2.2 %, induced drag within 0.4 %.

blocks.html_en: • Control surfaces followed thin-airfoil theory at any deflection. With control.chordFrac (c_f/c) set, two DATCOM corrections are added (sec. 6.1.1.1, digitised in Roskam Part VI): the viscous one (a real surface is weaker than theory) and the nonlinear K'(δ) for large deflections. The method reproduces NACA TR 661 (23012, 0.2c flap) to ±0.03 in Δc_l up to 20°. Set for the Cessna aileron, elevator and rudder.

blocks.html_en: • The gust hit the whole aircraft at once. It was a uniform vertical wind, so the tail felt it together with the wing. Now a gust is frozen in the air (sim.gustAt): the aircraft flies through it, and every strip of the wing and the tail sees it at its own position — the tail l_t/V later. That is how the rules' gust alleviation factor is derived.

blocks.html_en: • Crew vibration in the stress programme. The vibration measure (ISO 2631, RMS over 2 s) is meant for sustained shaking; gusts and abrupt controls are one-off jolts, already assessed by the g-load by axis and the Brinkley impact model. In this programme vibration is measured only in steady flight between manoeuvres (a note in the report says so). The recovery after each manoeuvre now starts with a smooth 1.5 s unload — the autopilot used to push from 3.7 g to 0.2 g in about a second.

    • Solved by the p-k method: at each speed the roots of the characteristic polynomial are found. Flutter is the speed where an oscillation stops decaying. Divergence is where torsion loses static stability.

blocks.html_en: • Cessna 172S: torsion box and strut are estimates (assumptions "Wing torsion box skin" and "Strut attachment"). There is no data: the Cessna structural repair manual (SESR04) gives only materials; there are no wing stiffnesses or frequency measurements. Spars at 20 and 65 % chord, skin 0.020 in, strut to the front spar at 2.6 m from the centerline, root hinged. Result: no wing flutter up to 270 m/s, divergence from 690 m/s for any combination of estimates (skin 0.016–0.025 in, spars ±5 % chord, strut ±0.3 m). This is a plausibility check: the aircraft is certified, and the regulations require freedom from flutter up to 1.2·V_D ≈ 112 m/s. Without the strut the same cantilever diverges at 192 m/s, and the first frequency drops from 12.8 to 6.5 Hz. Aileron flutter (on the real aircraft they are mass-balanced) is not computed.

blocks.html_en: • Flutter frequency. 8–13 % higher than the real one, even with four modes: the cause is strip theory (no tip losses), not the number of modes. NACA's 1949 calculation with the same theory gave the same error: 25.27 Hz vs. 22.1. The flutter speed still agrees.

sentences.en: Flutter frequency.
8–13 % higher than the real one, even with four modes: the cause is strip theory (no tip losses), not the number of modes.
NACA's 1949 calculation with the same theory gave the same error: 25.27 Hz vs. 22.1.
The flutter speed still agrees.

blocks.html_en: • Natural frequencies. The clamp in the model is perfectly rigid; the real one in the tunnel is more compliant.

sentences.en: Natural frequencies.
The clamp in the model is perfectly rigid; the real one in the tunnel is more compliant.

blocks.html_en: • Laminate strength is overestimated. A calculation based on the failure strain of a unidirectional ply (1.58 %) does not know that fibers in a laminate break earlier: a quasi-isotropic one fails at 1.25 %. This is a known effect: stress concentration at specimen edges, cracking of neighboring plies, interlaminar stresses at free edges. So the model rates parts with a layup as stronger than real ones — by up to 20 %. No correction factor was fitted.

sentences.en: Laminate strength is overestimated.

blocks.html_en:
• Blades on flapping hinges (flapping on the rotor). This is how the R22 hub is built per the POH: teetering, with coning hinges.
    • Each blade's flapping has its own equation: Iβ·β̈ = M_aero + M_grav − Iβ·Ω²·(β₀ + β). Centrifugal force restores the blade at exactly once per revolution.
    • The blade stays a rigid body in Rapier. Flapping is superimposed on the position and velocity of the sections in the aerodynamics and loads, and the moment about the hinge is removed from the body — it is not transmitted to the hub.
    • Coning settles by itself: 1.8° in hover (the previous constant-coning estimate was 2°).
    • Blade loads include the blade's acceleration due to flapping (angular, centripetal, Coriolis).

Why it diverges

blocks.html_en: • Phugoid period. In the test the yoke was released and the elevator is free: it "floats", and the stability margin is smaller than with a fixed elevator. With a smaller margin the phugoid is longer. In addition, propeller slipstream over the tail is not accounted for.

sentences.en: Phugoid period.
In the test the yoke was released and the elevator is free: it "floats", and the stability margin is smaller than with a fixed elevator.
With a smaller margin the phugoid is longer.
In addition, propeller slipstream over the tail is not accounted for.

blocks.html_en: • Spiral. The model's lateral stability (C_lβ) is 1.4 times lower than computed, so bank from sideslip builds more slowly. How many degrees of rudder 2 cm of pedal gives is an estimate (≈ 3°): with 4° the model reaches 30° bank in 17 s. On the real aircraft the ailerons are free as well.

sentences.en: Spiral.
The model's lateral stability (C_lβ) is 1.4 times lower than computed, so bank from sideslip builds more slowly.
How many degrees of rudder 2 cm of pedal gives is an estimate (≈ 3°): with 4° the model reaches 30° bank in 17 s.
On the real aircraft the ailerons are free as well.

blocks.html_en: • Directional stability C_nβ. It is higher than the NASA and JSBSim calculations. But a fin of 1.73 m² (Jane's) with "end-plate aspect ratio" and sidewash per the DATCOM breakdown gives 0.1–0.15. The propeller normal force in sideslip, which reduces directional stability, is not computed in the model.

blocks.html_en: Cessna 172S fixed-pitch propeller: engine–propeller rpm equilibrium (2026-11-12)

sentences.en: Cessna 172S fixed-pitch propeller: engine–propeller rpm equilibrium (2026-11-12)

blocks.html_en: A continuation of the fifth review: the largest divergence there was the Cessna climb (+49 % at sea level, +60 % at 8000 ft). The cause was known: the propeller in the model is a momentum disk with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller has no set rpm. The rpm settles where engine torque equals the torque the propeller absorbs. At low speed the propeller is "heavier", rpm is below 2700, and the engine delivers less power. The rule is the same: the references are only independent 172S POH data (data/research.md, part 4.2), nothing was tuned to fit them.

blocks.html_en: • src/core/propeller.ts (new) — a blade element propeller model with momentum theory on each annulus: axial and tangential induced velocities, Prandtl tip and root losses. At each radius a single equation is solved for the inflow angle φ (the Ning 2014 formulation, written for a propeller): Ωr·(sin²φ − σ'·Cn/4F) − V·(sin φ·cos φ + σ'·Ct/4F) = 0. There is no singularity at V = 0; the root is found by bisection. Section coefficients come from the shared airfoilCoeffs model (full range of angles, Prandtl–Glauert, compressibility drag rise from the sixth review). There is propellerEquilibrium — the equilibrium rpm for a given engine torque.

There is no singularity at V = 0; the root is found by bisection.

blocks.html_en: • src/core/sim.ts — the propeller drive has an optional fixedPitch block. If it is set, rpm is a state variable: I·dΩ/dt = Q_engine − Q_prop. Engine torque = throttle × power/ω_rated × altitude lapse. Without the block everything is as before (a disk with an efficiency — like a constant-speed propeller; projects from design.ts are built this way). At zero throttle the propeller windmills and brakes the aircraft. Sample has propRpm, propEfficiency.

blocks.html_en: • IO-360-L2A engine. At full throttle torque is constant and power is proportional to rpm. The basis is type certificate EASA.IM.E.032 (Issue 03, 2022, sec. 6 "Ratings", full throttle at sea level): 119 kW (160 hp) at 2400 rpm and 134 kW (180 hp) at 2700 rpm. That is 474 N·m at both points, to within 0.1 % (data/research.md, 4.2, item 7). Below 2400 rpm there are no data points; constant torque there is an assumption. New field powerplant.ratedRpm = 2700.

blocks.html_en: • Flight program (programs.ts). At full throttle in level flight at sea level the fixed-pitch propeller would spin the engine up to 3080 rpm. So the program, like a pilot, pulls back the throttle and holds no more than ratedRpm: the 2700 redline (POH, section 2). Maximum speed is now under this limit, which is how the POH defines its 126 kt. New fields in the flight results: vMaxRpm, cruiseRpm, cruisePropEfficiency, climbRpm, climbPropEfficiency. No other aircraft have fixedPitch; nothing changed for them.

blocks.html_en: How the compressibility drag rise (sixth review, merged in parallel) affected these numbers: without it static rpm was 3105, climb — 991 and 588 fpm, absorbed power — −19 %. What this means

blocks.html_en:
• Climb: the divergence shrank from +49…+60 % to +17…+18 %. It remains for three reasons, each pushing the same way.
    1. The model propeller is "light": at the same speed and rpm it absorbs 10–23 % less power than the real one, most of all at low J. Climb rpm is therefore higher than it would be with the real propeller, and the engine delivers more power.
    2. Propeller efficiency in the climb is 0.68–0.71. Estimates from the POH put the real one at about 0.6–0.65. The model lacks flow blockage by the cowling and the increase in fuselage drag in the propeller slipstream.
    3. The model airframe needs less power than the real one: the parasite drag area of 0.36 m² is an estimate.

blocks.html_en: • The "light" propeller is probably the geometry. The blade angle is known only through the 60 in pitch. What it is measured from (the flat side or the chord) and where the airfoil's zero lift lies are estimates. At J ≈ 0.7 the sections operate at an angle of attack of about 1°, and a 1° error changes absorbed power by about 15 %. For the static case, the sensitivity is printed in the divergence reason: with chord ×1.25 (AF 100, also a typical value) it would be 2315 rpm, with c_l,max 1.6 — 2192. I did not change the chord: that would be fitting to the number being checked. There is also a sign that it is not only the geometry: the APC 9x4.7 SF propeller, built from UIUC measured geometry, also falls short on C_T and C_P by 20–26 % in static conditions (the "small propeller" section). Outside the experiment I ran the same APC through the new solver: C_T 0.095, C_P 0.036, FM 0.651. The previous model of blades as Rapier bodies gave 0.644 — two different implementations agree.

blocks.html_en: src/core/aero.ts, dynamicStall: a vortex following the Beddoes–Leishman scheme was added to the pressure lag (Tp) and separation lag (Tf). The vorticity C_V is the difference between the attached-flow normal force and the force with lagged separation (in the scheme C_N^C·(1 − K_N)); its increments feed into the vortex normal force with lag Tv while the vortex is over the airfoil (τ_v ≤ Tvl from stall onset by the criterion). Then the vortex force decays with Tv/2; if stall continues, after Tvl + Tsh the next vortex begins (Tsh = 2(1 − w)/St). Stall onset is the lagged angle beyond the static stall angle, i.e. C_N1 is the static stall normal force. The constants are the published ones for NACA 0012, not tuned to the references: Tp 1.7, Tf 3.0, Tv 6.0 (Leishman & Beddoes; the same numbers are the OpenFAST AeroDyn defaults), Tvl 7.0 (Leishman & Beddoes 1986 for NACA 0012 at M 0.3; the OpenFAST default is 11), St 0.19. Not introduced: the Tf and Tv corrections by cycle stage (multipliers 0.25…4 in OpenFAST), the vortex suction force and pitching moment. It acts only on parts with unsteady flow — that is, flapping wings; propellers, airplanes and helicopters are not affected.

blocks.html_en: The Snowbird verdict is still "Does not fly". The vortex closed about a sixth of the thrust gap. According to the loop comparison, at the Snowbird wingtip Re the model underestimates the mean normal force by 9–28 % (most of all when pitching from 0 to 20°, as at the wingtip) and the peak by 25–35 % — enough to explain a noticeable part of the remaining gap, but not all of it: the model also underestimates gliding drag by 22 % (i.e. in flight the real wing needs even more thrust than the model). What else is not accounted for in Snowbird: the bending and twist of the real spar along the span (the model has a hinge at 6 m and linear twist), the DT-HPO1 airfoil instead of NACA 0012 (the stall constants are for NACA 0012), ground effect on thrust.

blocks.html_en: The coefficients were taken from a measurement of the airfoil itself, not of a rotor: two-dimensional NACA 0012 in the Langley LTPT tunnel (Carpenter, NACA TN 4357, fig. 5). M_dd (where dc_d/dM = 0.1) at α = 0, 4, 6, 8° fell on the line 0.800 − 0.31·c_l with a scatter of ±0.02, i.e. κ_A = 0.92, s = 0.31. Korn's classic s = 0.1 is for airfoils at their design c_l; for a loaded NACA 0012 M_dd drops three times faster (with that s, Korn–Lock at α = 4–8° gave almost no rise where c_d had already doubled in the experiment). The −t/c term is confirmed by the text of the same report: a blade with an NACA 0015 tip diverges at a c̄_l 0.10 lower than NACA 0012, and 0.03 of thickness = 0.31 × 0.10.

blocks.html_en: Primary source — Leishman and Syal's work (JAHS 2008; derivations and figures are in Syal's master's thesis, UMD 2008, which is downloadable). There κ_int is the ratio of the induced power of the pair to two isolated rotors at the same disk loading, i.e. the same definition as in the model. Momentum theory gives 1.281 if the lower rotor is in the fully contracted wake of the upper one: this is the lowest possible value. If the rotors are in the same plane — 1.414. For both Harrington rotors Leishman and Syal use 1.28. An independent measurement — Cameron, Karpatne, Sirohi (J. Aircraft 2016): upper rotor +18 %, lower +49 %, 1.33 on average. The value 1.16 (from a forum) is below the theoretical minimum; it was not found in the primary sources.

blocks.html_en: • The coaxial rotor rig assembled the upper rotor incorrectly (hoverRig in validation.ts, a bug from the fifth check). For the mirrored blade (clockwise rotor) the root was placed on the other side of the axis, and the blade went through the axis. Such a rotor produced 4.5 times less thrust. The fifth check compared the experiment against a pair in which mostly one rotor was producing thrust. With the fixed rig and the old κ_int = 1.16, Harrington rotor 1 gives −7…−14 % instead of −14…−26 %: at low thrust the rig bug was the main cause, at high thrust — κ_int. The helicopter builder (design.ts) and the quadcopter preset place the blade correctly; the bug did not affect them.

blocks.html_en: R22: compressibility is not the main cause. According to measurements on a rotor with the same airfoil (TN 3850), the compressibility power rise at M_t 0.71 is only 4.4 %, and the R22 has M_t 0.60–0.67 (104 % rpm, −20…+40 °C) — even less. In the model it added about 1 % to the R22 (−20 °C: −12.0 → −11.1 %). The model even computes the rotor itself 5 % more expensive than the experiment (the same TN 3850 at low M_t). So the 11–13 % lies outside blade aerodynamics: the downwash load on the cabin (2–5 % of thrust) is not accounted for; the tail rotor and transmission share (15 %) is an estimate; interpreting the steep portion of the POH chart as the takeoff 131 BHP is also an estimate. None of these numbers was tuned to the POH.

blocks.html_en: What this means for the verdicts

sentences.en: What this means for the verdicts

blocks.html_en: • Cessna. The model describes steady flight within 4–9 % in power, and stall accurately. Climb is strongly overestimated (+50–60 %): in the model the propeller is a disc with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed. A real fixed-pitch propeller at low speed turns below 2700 rpm, with an efficiency of about 0.6. The "Does not fly" verdicts for an overloaded aircraft are therefore optimistic: the model may pass an aircraft that in reality will not climb.

sentences.en: Cessna.
The model describes steady flight within 4–9 % in power, and stall accurately.
Climb is strongly overestimated (+50–60 %): in the model the propeller is a disc with a constant efficiency of 0.85, and the engine at full throttle delivers full power at any speed.
A real fixed-pitch propeller at low speed turns below 2700 rpm, with an efficiency of about 0.6.
The "Does not fly" verdicts for an overloaded aircraft are therefore optimistic: the model may pass an aircraft that in reality will not climb.

blocks.html_en: • Rotors in hover. The model with κ = 1.15 correctly describes a twisted rotor (Carpenter, within 5 %) and the Harrington single rotor. For an untwisted rotor and at low Reynolds numbers (TN 626) it underestimates power by 4–11 %. For the real R22 the discrepancy is 12 %. Known causes: no compressibility drag rise at the blade tip (M 0.62–0.65; for the Carpenter rotor at M 0.7 FM is 10 % lower than at M 0.3), no download from the wake on the cabin (2–5 % of thrust), the tail rotor and transmission share of 15 % is an estimate. The model R22 hovers where the real one no longer can: its hover ceiling is optimistic by roughly 2000–2500 ft.

sentences.en: Rotors in hover.
The model with κ = 1.15 correctly describes a twisted rotor (Carpenter, within 5 %) and the Harrington single rotor.
For an untwisted rotor and at low Reynolds numbers (TN 626) it underestimates power by 4–11 %.
For the real R22 the discrepancy is 12 %.

Known causes: no compressibility drag rise at the blade tip (M 0.62–0.65; for the Carpenter rotor at M 0.7 FM is 10 % lower than at M 0.3), no download from the wake on the cabin (2–5 % of thrust), the tail rotor and transmission share of 15 % is an estimate.
The model R22 hovers where the real one no longer can: its hover ceiling is optimistic by roughly 2000–2500 ft.

blocks.html_en: • Coaxial rotors (outdated — see the sixth check: κ_int = 1.28, and the coaxial rotor test stand had been assembled with an error). κ_int = 1.16 was taken from a forum; the primary source was not read. Harrington's experiment shows that a coaxial pair takes 1.22–1.37 times more power than two separate rotors at half thrust each, while the model gives about 1.12. The hover power of the Ka-26 and Ka-32 in the model is probably underestimated by 10–20 %. The value 1.16 was not changed: there is no reliable number to replace it (in Harrington's data the split into profile and induced parts is unstable, rotor 1 is wooden, with very low solidity). A comparison with Harrington's second rotor and with the primary source is needed.

blocks.html_en: • Post-stall (the "Dune" ornithopter, blades in reverse flow) the model underestimates aerodynamic forces at 30–60° by 10–20 %.

sentences.en: Post-stall (the "Dune" ornithopter, blades in reverse flow) the model underestimates aerodynamic forces at 30–60° by 10–20 %.

blocks.html_en: • Flapping-wing aircraft. The model describes SmartBird's shaft power within the accuracy of the paper. Snowbird with the real kinematics does not stay airborne in the model: thrust is a third of drag, and gliding drag is 22 % less than measured. On the real wing the tip operates at ±20–23° — in the dynamic-stall regime, where lift is sustained by the leading-edge stall vortex. The model did not have this vortex; it does now, but the discrepancy remains (see "Seventh physics check"). The verdict for large slow flapping-wing aircraft ("Does not fly") is therefore pessimistic.

Found and fixed

blocks.html_en: • Cruise power was taken before the flight condition had settled (programs.ts, flight program). Power was averaged over 22–30 s after leaving the maximum speed. The speed controller (0.08 per m/s) was still oscillating by then, with a period of about 40 s. At 112 knots at 8000 ft it gave 78 kW instead of the steady-state 76, and at neighbouring speeds the curve jumped. Now the cruise controller is damped (0.25 per m/s), and power is taken only when for 16 s in a row the speed stays within 0.2 m/s, altitude does not change and throttle does not wander. If it has not settled within 200 s, the report says so. The old comparison at 124 knots: was 96.3 kW, now 93.7 kW.

blocks.html_en: • The altitude controller of the "Takeoff and hover" program oscillated at low density. For the R22 at 1524 m altitude wandered by ±3 m with a period of about 9 s, the hover was not counted, and the mean power was biased. The old "R22 at 5000 ft" comparison (85.3 kW) relied on this. The inner loop (collective → acceleration) is slower at low density, and the outer one was too stiff. The altitude and speed gains of 1.0 and 1.8 were replaced with 0.4 and 1.2. Oscillation for the R22: at sea level 1.2 → 0.55 m, at 1524 m 6.2 → 1.9 m (hover counted), at 3000 m 3.5 → 1.7 m; for the quadcopter and Ka-26 no worse than before. For comparisons with the POH, hover is still computed on a fixed body, with the collective pitch trimmed for thrust equal to weight.

blocks.html_en: • Item 1 and the Ka-32. The false "Breaks up" for the Ka-32 from data/gen-live/ka32.json was caused not by the unidirectional web but by item 1. At 3.8° coning the blade's 297 kN centrifugal force should relieve the shear from thrust (18 kN), but the model put the entire thrust into the web. Hence a shear stress of 37.5 MPa against a strength of 40 MPa. Now 2.9 MPa. A ±45° laminate web model was not needed for this verdict. The webs are still unidirectional, and the shear and buckling estimate for them is conservative.

blocks.html_en: • Item 2. The error is in the engine itself and shows on any body made of several colliders. Now the body's mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor are summed in the stand (parallel axis theorem, principal axes by the Jacobi method) and passed to Rapier ready-made; a single-part body has nothing to sum — the mass sits on its collider, as before. Ornithopters are unaffected: each of their bodies is a single part.

The error is in the engine itself and shows on any body made of several colliders.

Now the body's mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor are summed in the stand (parallel axis theorem, principal axes by the Jacobi method) and passed to Rapier ready-made; a single-part body has nothing to sum — the mass sits on its collider, as before.

blocks.html_en: • Item 5. Damping is by strips, with the cantilever's first mode shape: ½·ρ·a·c·U·F(k) per metre of span, U = Ω·r for a blade and the flow speed for a wing, F(k) is the Theodorsen function. The added mass ρπc²/4 lowers the first frequency of a light wing: for SmartBird 52.7 → 37.1 Hz. The "close to resonance" warning is now issued only if the gain is at least 1.5. The coaxial Ka-26 and Ka-32 have ζ ≈ 0.45 and gain ×1.1–1.2: no warning. The R22 has ζ = 0.26 and ×2.0: the warning remains. For a real articulated blade (ν = 1, γ/16 ≈ 0.25) this is the same.

SmartBird: mean moment 0.005 N·m (moment coefficient 0.003) — a small tail can provide it; alternating ±0.29 N·m at the flapping frequency — without holding, the body would rock by about ±14°. Snowbird: −8.3 N·m (−0.01) and ±116 N·m, about ±5°. This does not change the verdict (the tail is not modelled), but it is stated. It was checked that the moment measured this way matches the hinge moment from Newton–Euler (difference 0.034 out of 147 N·m).
